Mr. L. S. RENE MORIN (St. Hyacinthe-Rouville) moved that the first report of the select standing committee on standing orders, reading as follows, be concurred in:
Your committee have considered an order of the house dated 15th February, viz:-
"That the select standing committee on standing orders be instructed to consider the advisability of amending the standing orders so that certain estimates may be referred to a committee and so that bills reported from a standing or select committee shall be placed on the order paper for third reading after having been sufficiently debated by the house."
Your committee recommend that, during the present session, the house may refer any of the estimates to a standing or special committee, concurrently with the committee of supply, but that none of the estimates shall be concurred in by the house until reported by the committee of supply.
Your committee further recommend that, during the present session, when any bill, other than a government bill, reported from any standing or special committee, shall have been considered at two sittings and not disposed of, it shall be placed on the order paper for third reading; and when called in pursuance thereof, the question "That the bill be now read a third time" shall be put by Mr. Speaker and decided without debate or amendment.

subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE OF CERTAIN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE-THIRD READINC OF BILLS
speechtext:
The order of reference to the select standing committee on standing orders was two-fold. The committee was instructed to consider the advisability of amending the rules of the house, first, to enable the house to refer the consideration of certain estimates to standing or special committees, and second, so that bills reported from a standing or select committee might be placed on the order paper for third reading after having been sufficiently debated by the house.
The purpose of the first part of the reference was to expedite the business of the house by referring the estimates of some of the departments which, under the present rules,

can only be dealt with by the house sitting in committee of the whole, to standing or special committees upon which concurrent jurisdiction would be conferred, in which committees fuller and more accprate information could be obtained from the officers of the departments familiar with the circumstances of each particular item than could reasonably be expected from a minister speaking offhand on the subject from his seat in the house. The results to be expected from this new procedure would be more accurate and secure fuller information for the benefit of hon. members; and secondly, the discussion in the house would be restricted to the really contentious items, the debates thereby being materially shortened.
The committee was of the opinion that rather than amend the rules of the house at once, it would be wiser to test the expediency of the new procedure by an experiment during one session, and its recommendation is that during the present session the house may refer any of the estimates to a standing or special committee, concurrently, with the committee of supply, such estimates, however, remaining subject to consideration and report by the committee of supply.
The object of the second1 part of the reference is again to expedite the business of the house and to enable it to give a decision on private and public legislation submitted to it after such legislation has been sufficiently debated.	: vl
The house expressed itself on this matter when, two years ago, with that definite purpose in view, it amended its rules by providing that private bills considered during the hour devoted to private bills on Tuesdays and Fridays, and not disposed of, would be placed at the foot of the list on the order paper.
But the rule resorted to has proved inadequate, and to remedy this situation the committee recommends that, as an experiment, a sessional order be passed providing that dhring the present session when any bill, other than a government bill, reported from any special or standing committee shall have been considered at two sittings, and not disposed of, it shall be placed o>n the order paper for third reading, and when called in pursuance thereof the question, "that the b;ll be now read the third time," shall be put by the Speaker and decided without debate or amendment.
The committee considered that after full and free debate on the second reading and before the special or standing committee to which the bill was referred and at two different sittings of the house sitting as a com-

subtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE OF CERTAIN ESTIMATES TO COMMITTEE-THIRD READINC OF BILLS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the report contains two recommendations, as the mover has said, but in them both there is evidence of a tendency to divest this house of a certain portion of its responsibilities and to hand them over to other bodies, sometimes to the cabinet, sometimes to boards, and sometimes, as in this case, to committees. But all these bodies to which we are invited to hand over our authority are not so directly responsible to the people as we .are, and they function in a way which prevents that desirable publicity being shed on their proceedings which is associated with our deliberations and actions in this chamber.
Now, there are two recommendations, and I propose to deal with them separately. The first one is to the effect that estimates may be sent to a special or standing committee, but it provides that those estimates must also go through our committee of the whole before they have any legislative sanction. It appears to me, sir, that on the face of it, if it does not go any further than that, it is a comparatively innocuous and, to tell the truth, a somewhat feeble suggestion. It reminds me of the epitaph on a tombstone in an old English graveyard erected to the memory of a three-day-old child. After stating the particulars of the infant's name and death this doggerel follows:
If so soon I would be done for,
What on earth was I begun for?
And it seems to me that if this innocuous recommendation does not really go any further, and is not intended to, what on earth was it begun for.
It will probably be said in the course of this debate, and correctly so, that this method of dealing with estimates has been a success in the case of the estimates for the Canadian National Railways. But the conditions are entirely different there from what they are in the action now proposed. The Canadian National Railway estimates represent what is entirely a national proposition. Broad policies are discussed, you have Sir Henry Thornton and his staff in attendance, and the leaders of the various groups in the house can readily agree whether the policy is a good one or not. But the other estimates are local estimates and so to speak, specialized; think of the thousand and one items that comprise the agricultural estimates, or those of the marine and fisheries or the Post Office Department -almost any of the estimates in fact other than the larger ones in connection with the national railways. Those items require local knowledge to illuminate them, as it were. As you know, the procedure now is for the minister to explain the reason for the estimate from the book that is placed in front of him. If further information is required, perhaps the over-burdened memory of the deputy minister is drawn on; but in the last analysis when it comes down to the giving of information for or against that particular item, is it not the member for the local district whose particular knowledge is relied on, and in the special committee that local knowledge will be lacking except as it may be furnished by the few members composing the committee. Now, if this proposal to send estimates to a private committee is to replace discussion in committee of the whole, then it is vicious, absolutely so. We are toldl that that is not now proposed, but I am very much afraid, sir, that it is the direction in which we will be heading if we adopt this recommendation. It is unreasonable in itself unless it is intended logically to go further.
However, to deal with what is absolutely before us, it is said to be concurrent; that is to say, that the discussion in the special committee will be additional to the discussion which will take place in this house. In that case it will be useless; if it is useless it will be wasteful and entirely unnecessary. Once upon a time an eastern potentate who had captured a city proposed to burn a valuable old library. On being remonstrated with he said: Either these books support the Koran or they are opposed to it. If they support it they are unnecessary; if they oppose it they are wicked. In either case they are superfluous. Thereupon he ordered the library to

Rules oj the House-Mr. Neill
be burned. Now, all we obtain from this recommendation, provided it is not intended to go any further, is that the overworked minister-'because he is 'busy at this season of the year-and his equally overworked deputy-who is also very busy-shall be compelled to go over all their estimates, one by one, in the fullest sense, twice, once in the special private committee-shall I call it the "hole-and-corner" committee?-and again in the full light of this house. What use will that be to anybody if the work is done twice? The answer has already been given by the mover, and will be given again: It will shorten debate in committee of the whole. That is all right, sir, as regards the estimates of the Canadian National Railways. When the three leaders in this house and the outstanding members of their parties tell us in committee of the whole, "We have looked at these estimates of the Canadian National Railways and are satisfied with them,'' I for one am quite prepared to accept their view, as I have no doubt are other members. But, as I say, the conditions are totally different with respect to what I call the local estimates. When it comes down to local matters affecting the coal mining, farming, logging and fishing interests of the constituency which I represent, I say emphatically, no; I will not surrender my right to discuss these matters; I will not surrender it to any lawyer from Winnipeg, any millionaire from Toronto, or any business man from Halifax, however worthy they may be; however much abler they are than I am in their particular spheres, they do not know the local conditions of the district I represent. I know that the time honoured gag will be trotted out-it is hoary headed in its hypocrisy: "Oh, but you can go before the committee and you will be allowed to speak there." How often have I not heard that advanced: You can go to the committee although you are not a member of it and you will be accorded a courteous hearing. Yes, you will be given a courteous hearing once; but when it comes down to butting in-to use a common expression-on every item and arguing the merits and taking an active part generally in the debate you will soon find that you are not wanted. Any member butting in-I cannot use any other word to express the idea-will find that he has as much weight there as the Hansard reporter has in the debates that take place in this chamber.
We are told that this would shorten the debate and save the precious time of the house. Well, that was the very bait that was held out to us two years ago when we sold our birthright of free speech, or a portion 
of it at any rate, for a mess of pottage. And a sorry looking mess the pottage was when we got it; to me it seemed more like the funeral baked meats of the ancient Egyptians. Certainly it was very much inferior to the life giving pottage of the days of Isaac and Esau, and indeed even inferior to what is supposed to be its lineal descendant, the brose of the modem Scot.
I would submit to the house in all seriousness that there are greater advantages to be gained by our considering every item in committee of the whole than by getting through quickly and going home, which is the main bait held out in this case. There are a good many members of this house, myself amongst them-and I am not ashamed to admit it-who exhibited great anxiety to come here and occupy the honourable position we hold, and who by hard fought campaigns and many promises secured this much sought boon. We told the people that we would do our duty to the last ditch, and so forth. Now are we getting tired and lazy? Do we want to shirk the obligations which we undertook when we came here? A few days, a week or two longer would not make any great difference. I would point out also, to put it bluntly that we are being paid for being here. I admit that the salary is quite incommensurate with the work we do, but at the same time we knew what the remuneration was when we sought the position, and if we are not satisfied to do the work for which we were sent here we should resign. I know there are scores of men in the district I represent fully as able and1 quite as willing to represent my constituency.
Another time-honoured gag will be trotted out for our delectation. When the report comes from the select private committee we shall be told1: "Now, this matter has been seriously and carefully-almost prayerfully- considered in the select committee and the house would be well advised to accept their just and wise verdict." I can recall that gag also; many a time have I heard it in this house. Let me give an illustration of what actually happened on One occasion, I was endeavouring in this house to have the report of a select committee changed. The committee had reported something and I wished to have their report amended. The chairman of the committee got up and in sonorous tones he got off the gag I have mentioned; the matter had been so carefully considered by the select committee that the house would be wise to follow that committee's "mature judgment". But this is what actually happened on that occasion. It was a small

Rules of the House-Mr. Neill
committee and the recommendation I wished was defeated by a vote of four to three. One of my friends on whom I had relied to support me was absent, however, and on my reproaching him afterwards with his absence he said he was very sorry but he had gone to have his hair cut; and because that hon. gentleman had gone to have his hair cut something of material importance to certain interests in the country had to stand over for a year or, perhaps, be abandoned altogether. That is the effect of accepting always the report of a small select standing committee.
The other night the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) and my desk mate the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) told us, and it was not denied, that we were railroading divorce bills through the house at a scandalous rate. I say, it cannot be denied. And why does that condition exist? It is just a logical and direct consequence of the very system now proposed. These divorce cases used to be considered in this house in committee of the whole, but we drifted into the dolce far niente method of leaving the whole question to a select committee, with the result that divorces are now rushed through without the slightest attention being paid them. That is the natural and inevitable consequence of the same sort of system proposed in this Connection,; only in this case we are beginning in a small way and comparatively gently.
I may point out that this very practice has been tried elsewhere before. It was tried in British Columbia when I was a member of the local house, and it was never tried again. I got my estimates through, it is true, but by a method which-I have not the time now to describe to the house. But it was not desirable; it led to log rolling, most of us know what that means. Now, if the system here proposed were to be adopted I might be tempted to approach some hon. members opposite-perhaps I might select my worthy and genial friend from New Westminster (Mr. McQuarrie), because at times he has evinced a certain amount of the milk of human kindness, and we are brother British Columbians-and I would say to him: " If you vote for the wise and just estimates for my district, I will vote for the rotten, unjust estimates for yours." It is to be hoped, of course, that neither the hon. member for New Westminster nor myself would yield to that temptation. Still, Mr. Speaker, you, yourself, deem it advisable every day at three o'clock to pray that we be delivered from temptation, and sometimes I wonder whether it would not be wise if you renewed the supplication at eight o'clock for fear the strength prayed for earlier in the day might have waned.
I will be nothing but frank; I admit that this recommendation as it stands, word for word, and not going 'beyond that in the slightest, is comparatively innocuous. Nevertheless it is a wedge; it is that fatal thing known to us in this house as a precedent. Why did we spend three days last week debating the question of grants for roads? We did so largely because we had this great thing behind us, precedent. Once enter the fatal path of precedent and it will soon lead us to all the evils I have suggested. Moreover it is not merely a question of passing estimates for this post office or that wharf or something else of the kind; what is valuable is the discussion that arises out of the estimates. Statements which the leaders, the cabinet ministers, hear in their offices, statements made in caucus, are almost entirely ex parte; are they not? But it is in the light of the publicity obtained in this house that the members of the cabinet get the cross current of public sentiment. It is of the greatest benefit to them, to us all and to the country at large to hear the discussions that take place even on some comparatively trivial item-arguments which would be all lost sight of in this private committee.
Let me now state my final objection to this particular recommendation. I am utterly opposed to what I call star chamber methods. There would be no Hansard in this private committee; no votes would be recorded but merely totals; no names would appear. It would be possible for the government or a member to speak one way on the hustings and vote another in the committee. I referred a moment ago to a friend who was absent from a meeting because he had to have his hair cut. Now, I do not wish to be cynical for a moment, but it might be said by those who are cynical that the government whip had suggested to him that his hair was a little long! Also it would be open to unscrupulous opponents to accuse a member of having cast a wrong vote in committee and he would not be able to prove its untruth; for a lie can always get ahead of the truth. I am very much afraid, not so much of this particular recommendation as of what it would logically lead to. Before long we will be putting our power of voting estimates into the hands of a private committee, a hole in the corner committee, one upon whose actions they cannot, will not and perhaps dare not let the God-given light of publicity shine.
'So much for that part of the report; I want now to deal with the second recommendation which is of much greater immediate importance. I refer to the recommendation with regard to the manner of dealing with private

Rules of the House-Mr. Neill
and public bills. We will do well to remember that this deals with both private and public bills; it may be a bill of a thousand pages, dealing with the Companies Act or with the Criminal Code, imposing some drastic restriction on the right of assembly or free speech. This is the course such a bill will pursue:	After going to this private committee, where no vote is recorded and where there is no Hansard, it will be brought back to this house on two separate occasions. We know that public and private bills come before this house for only one hour on two evenings a week. It may be said that the bill may be brought up on Monday and discussed all day, but if there were any suspicion that a bill would be opposed very strenuously it would not be brought up on that day. It might be brought up at ten minutes to nine or it might be brought up at ten minutes after eight; strike an average and say it would be up for one hour altogether. Two advocates of the bill may speak on it; each is entitled to speak for forty minutes, so there will not be much left of the hour. Some hon. members may have some important amendments to offer, of which they nfay have given notice; the advocates of the bill, knowing that, could make it their business to talk out the bill, and at the end of the hour it would come to the house for third reading. That would be bad enough, but it becomes much worse. The next time the bill comes up it stands for third reading, and it is proposed that there can be no amendment and no debate on the third reading; you cannot put anyone on record from the second reading until the bill has gone through. Many members vote for the second reading of a bill with the idea of offering amendments in committee, but under this system we will never get the opinions of different members because bills will be talked out of committee on to third reading with no debate and no amendments allowed.
I am anticipating the arguments which may be brought forward in favour of this method. It will be said, "Oh, he is depicting an extreme case; these things are not done now, because the good sense of the house will not allow them." Will it not? Let me remind hon. members that two years ago I was opposing the establishment of the forty minute rule;
I pointed out that if two or three obstructive questions were asked the member's time would be cut into seriously, and the answer given was that this would not 'be done, that time would be allowed) for interruptions. Upon that understanding perhaps many members agreed to the forty minute rule, but has that been the case? It has not; the rules are strictly
[Mr. Neill.3
enforced, and quite properly so once we adopted them, so do not let us be beguiled by the suggestion that the rule reads one way but that we will be allowed to do something else.
There is one other feature of the matter to which I would like to direct the attention of the house. This rule will be introduced immediately, and there are two important private bills coming up this session, the Sun Life bill and the Bell Telephone bill. I think I voted for one of them last year, so I am not particularly antagonistic to them, but I can see what may happen to these bills and I am opposed to it. When they were brought in the other day on second reading there was practically no debate, in the expectation that the debate would take place in committee of the whole. Now, unannounced, we will be deprived of that right; we cannot go back and debate the bills on second reading, so all we have (before us is two short periods of perhaps ten minutes each, after which the bills stand for third reading without debate. If this iniquitous rule is to be adopted let us at least send it back to the committee with instructions that it shall not take effect until next session.
I frankly admit that the rules were abused last session; these and other bills were deliberately obstructed. There is hardly a privilege we enjoy which is not subject to abuse at times, but because 10 per cent of the members abuse a privilege are we to deprive the other 90 per cent of their rights? Social conventions do not allow us to steal up behind a man and knock him down because we do not like the colour of his hair or the tie he wears; it is held that that is too drastic a remedy, and I submit that this rule is also too drastic for the difficulty it assumes to correct.
It may be said that I am merely offering destructive criticism, but that is not the case; I can easily suggest an appropriate remedy for the obstruction which undoubtedly occurred last year. I suggest simply the use of the rule we have had for many years, that is, the closure; that is the correct thing to do in such a case, simply put on closure. Almost every government in the world has the closure rule in some form or other, but some hon. members will say that closure is objectionable. Why, this is simply Ossa piled upon Pelion, with respect to closure; this is a hundred times worse than closure heaped up, pressed down and running over. Under closure you must give notice, and the debate can continue until two o'clock the following morning; each member is limited to twenty

Privilege-Mr. Edwards (Frontenac)
minutes, so that thirty or forty men may speak, but here we will be limited to perhaps two speakers. And as an aside, may I draw attention to the incoherent condition of our rules at present owing to the way we tinkered with them two years ago. Now we have one rule which says we can take a vote under closure at two o'clock in the morning and another which says we must stop the debate at eleven o'clock. Our mess of pottage is all spattered up with red tape like the seals on a Christmas parcel.
I hope the house will reject this motion altogether. The first part is only weakly evil, but it has potentialities of harm which make it undesirable; the second part is wholly poisonous and destructive, subversive of the right of free speech, both propositions are unsound in principle and will be unworkable in practice. I fully believe that not one-half the members of this house knew this question was coming up to-day, and not half of them have been made acquainted with the effect these recommendations will have if adopted, so in order to give the government and hon. members on both sides of the house an opportunity to see what they are voting on, I am going to move that this debate be adjourned. I have not solicited anyone to second my motion, but if anyone cares to do so in order that the matter may be discussed better in their caucuses or in some other way, they may do so. I move the adjournment of the debate.

My attention has been
called to a short article appearing in a paper called the Edmonton Journal which indicates one of two things; either that paper is engulfed in the most profound ignorance, or it has a disregard for the truth. The article is headed " Changes his stand " and reads as follows:
Hon. Doctor J. W. Edwards, M.P., who led previous opposition to the western provinces securing their natural resources, free from any restriction, surprised the commons on Monday by moving a resoltion which will facilitate Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta securing a speedy return of their domains.
It is very hard for me to believe that any paper in Canada could be so ignorant of the facts. The article states that I led the opposition to the western provinces securing their natural resources, but page 360 of Hansard of February 16, 1927, shows that I moved the following resolution:
That in the opinion of this house, it is in the general interest of this Dominion that their natural resources should be transferred to the prairie provinces at the earliest possible moment, and that such transfer should not interfere with, restrict or modify the right of said provinces to complete control of their educational or other local affairs.
In my judgment that resolution is a complete contradiction of the article, and that contradiction is supported by a statement made by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) that,
"The agreement would be subject to the qualification that dt should not interfere with, restrict or modify the right of the province



Preservation oj Niagara Falls
to the complete control of its educational or other local affairs. That is where the disagreement comes in."
I was not attempting to restrict the transfer in any way, as is evidenced by the words of the resolution I then moved and by the remarks of the Minister of Justice.
I would also refer to Hansard of March 26, 1928, at page 1688 where I moved exactly the same resolution which this house saw fit to adopt unanimously last week. Word for word, comma for comma, the resolution compares with the one unanimously adopted by this house.
Whether this article is maliciously intended or not, it does me a grave injustice and is absolutely contrary to fact.

subtopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF CONVENTION WITH UNITED STATES

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved:
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF CONVENTION WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext:
That it is expedient that parliament do approve of the convention and protocol for the preservation of Niagara falls by the construction of remedial works and for the experimental wthdrawal of additional water from the Niagara river, which was signed at Ottawa, on the second day of January, nineteen hundred and twenty-nine, on behalf of His Majesty for the Dominion of Canada by the plenipotentiary named therein, and that this house do approve of the same;
And that a message be sent to the senate to acquaint their honours that this house unites wth the senate in the approval of the above-mentioned convention and protocol;
And that the clerk of the house do carry the said message to the senate.
He said: The convention ensures adequate measures for the preservation of the greatest scenic asset of America, and in addition provides a considerable supply of power in Ontario and New York on an experimental basis during the winter season when the water is most needed for power and least needed for scenic purposes.
Preliminary negotiations with respect to this convention were conducted on behalf of the government of Canada by the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) and on behalf of the United States government by the Hon. Mr. Kellogg and the Hon. Mr. Hoover. The Canadian government acted throughout in the closest cooperation with the government of Ontario and the Hydro-Electric Commission, both with respect to the various steps taken and with respect to the convention itself. I shall leave to the hon. Minister of the Interior the major presentation and discussion

of this matter, but it may facilitate an understanding of the one or two outstanding features of the convention and the circumstances which led to its being formulated, if I make a more or less formal statement.
In 1925-26 correspondence took place between the governments of Canada and the United States regarding the danger to the scenic properties of Niagara falls through the erosion of the escarpment. It was decided to appoint a commission to examine into this question and also into the question of the amount of water which might without injury be diverted for power purposes. The Special International Niagara Board was set up accordingly in October, 1926, and was constituted as follows:
J. T. Johnston, director of Dominion Water Power and Reclamation Service, Department of the Interior, Ottawa.
Dr. Charles Camsell, Deputy Minister of Mines, Ottawa, Major D. C. Jones, United States District Engineer at Buffalo.
Dr. J. Horace Macfarland, past president, American Civic Association, chairman of the Fine Arts Commission of Pennsylvania.
Mr. Johnston and Major Jones were the members of the International Board of Control established in 1923 to supervise and control the diversion of water authorized under article V of the Boundary Waters treaty of 1909.
Dr. Camsell was specially qualified to deal with the geological factors involved in a study of the recession of the falls, and Dr. Macfarland has been for many years a leader in the movement for the preservation of all natural scenic beauties. The services of specialists in the analysis of colour and light effects were also secured.
The special board has presented an interim report, which has been published by the Department of the Interior, and is completing its final report, which will present the technical details on which the recommendations were based.
The board found that the scenic qualities of the falls were being injured by various factors:
(i)	The natural recession of the falls through the eating away of the crest, which has been going on since prehistoric times and which measurements since 1842 show to have been at the average rate of 3.7 feet a year in the Horseshoe falls;
(ii)	Variations in the level of the lakes;

Preservation oj Niagara Falls
(iii)	Withdrawal of water for power purposes.
The board, however, found that there was no basis for the fear that the Horseshoe falls was likely to disappear through the deepening of the notch in the centre. The chief injury lay in the baring of the flanks of the crest line and the thinning of the sheet in certain parts. They concluded that with adequate supervision and control the scenic beauty of the falls could be preserved in perpetuity and that by suitable remedial works, particularly excavations and submerged weirs, the water could be distributed over the bared flanks, erosion modified and the present scenic beauty enhanced.
The works proposed were estimated to cost $1,750,000. Following the publication of the boards report, the Hydro Electric Power Commission of Ontario and the Niagara Falls Power Company of New York submitted an offer to construct the works recommended, under government control, conditional upon their being allowed to utilize, during the winter season only, 10,000 cubic feet of water per second on each side of the river in addition to the diversion permitted under the Boundary Waters treaty. The special Niagara board reviewed this offer and recommended its acceptance with some amendments, limiting this experimental diversion to seven years and providing for continuous regulation by the International Board of Control, with ' supervision by the special board of four members of the effect of the construction of the remedial works and the experimental withdrawals.

20,000	cubic feet of water a second and Canada to 32,000 second cubic feet, of which Canada exports 12,000 cubic feet of water a second. The result is that when this treaty is passed and the quantities are totalled, the United States will have 20,000 plus 12,000 plus a new
10,000,	or a total of 42,000 cubic feet of water a second while Canada will receive only 32,000 less 12,000 plus 10,000, or a total of 30,000 cubic feet of water a second. It is extremely problematical whether these remedial works will, from an engineering standpoint, have the effect which it is said they are going to have.
What I fear is this: the report says:
All the plans for remedial works hitherto suggested have contemplated replenishing the flow over the flanks of the Horseshoe fall and in the American channel and at the head of Goat island.
Now they are going to divert the water out of the Horseshoe falls. The main flow of water is on the Canadian side, and Canada is entitled to that waiter and the power developed from that flowing water. She is not, however, going to get it, according to the figures I have given. I am afraid they are going to get that water over to replenish the American falls and make it more beautiful at the expense of Canada, because Canada is not being properly protected and safeguarded. The report says:
Certain plans, including those for the construction of a curved weir across the main part of the rapids above the Horseshoe, and those for distributing the flow by numerous islands in the rapids, have had for their main object a radical reduction in the heavy flow over the central part of the Horseshoe. The premises upon which the assumed necessity for such a reduction has been based are:
First: That the American falls are more beautiful than the Horseshoe-
In my opinion that is not correct.
-and that consequently the general effect would be enhanced by thinning out the latter so as to make it similar to the former;
Second: That the Horseshoe is in danger of committing suicide and that the proposed thinning out would materially check the erosion; and

The treaty is no doubt all1 right as regards the legal side of it and the question of policy, but I feel we are being goldr-bricked and I am objecting to some of the details. What I fear is that they will get this Water out of the Horseshoe falls; it will go down by Goat island and on to the American falls, which have dried up and they will beautify and replenish the American falls at the expense of the Horseshoe and of Canada. If these remedial works are going to have the effect which, in my opinion, Canada should have, there should be additional safeguards in this agreement. From an engineering standpoint, the main flow of water will be diverted from the Horseshoe falls over to the American falls and the people of the United States will get the water. If we are going to preserve the beauty of the falls, why was a treaty not made

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while the reference and the report as issued by the special Niagara board are supposed to deal, and do deal, primarily with the preservation of the scenic beauty of Niagara falls, the main urge, I declare, is the question of power. The state of New York and the body in the state of New York that was especially created to protect the scenic interests, the Niagara State Reservation, own the bed of the Niagara river from the international boundary to the American side. They also own, and claim to own, the water, and they get a rental for the water. On this side of the river, from the boundary to the Canadian side, the bed of the river in front of the park is owned and vested in the Niagara Parks Commission, and they also get a rental for the water. They also own the water; that is the claim, and it is not disputed.
This new special Niagara board, which was appointed, as the Prime Minister says, in October, 1926, worked for one year and two months on this proposition of preserving the scenic beauty of Niagara, and during all that time they never thought it worth their while to consult with the state authorities of New York, as represented by the government of that state, nor with the State Reservation authorities. I am not going to refer particularly to the fact that during that year and a half, although the Niagara Park Commission was especially appointed for the preservation and conservation of both the falls and the gorge, this special board took up only twenty minutes of our engineer's time in that year and a half, or year and a quarter.
I want the house to know how the state of New York feels about this situation. I know that the Prime Minister will say that
the province of Ontario is satisfied because he had a letter from the premier of Ontario saying that he was satisfied. But the point I want to make clear to the house is this, that the urge is power, because these gentlemen never applied for any assistance to the people who are especially endowed with knowledge as to the conservation of the falls. On the contrary, they immediately applied themselves to the power people, and they made their arrangement at once with the HydroElectric Power Commission of Ontario, and with a privately owned power corporation on the other side. Let me show how the governor of the state of New York feels about this question. A few days ago under date of February 11, 1929, that is this month, he addressed a letter to Senator Wagner, regarding the water diversion at Niagara falls. He says:
I have delayed answering your letter of February 2nd for several days because it brings up a matter very vital to the interests of the people of the state of New York.
You ask me three specific questions in regard to the attitude of this state concerning the convention signed -at Ottawa between representatives of the United States and the government of Canada in relation to the diversion of water in the Niagara river above Niagara falls.
This convention is intended primarily to preserve the scenic beauty of Niagara falls by preventing rapid erosion of the centre of the crest of the falls through erection of weirs or other structures in the bed of the river above the falls on both the New York side and the Ontario side, thus diverting sufficient water to the wings of the falls.
This convention is the result of careful study made by the International Niagara Board, and this board worked out a plan under which an offer of the Hydro-Electric Power Commission of Ontario and the Niagara Falls Power Company, a private corporation of New York state, was recommended for acceptance. Under this offer the Ontario commission and the New York private corporation agreed to build the necessary weirs and structures in the bed of the river and asked in return the use, for a period of seven years, during the six winter months of each year, of 10,000 cubic feet per second of water on each side of the river. It is estimated that this 10,000 cubic feet per second on the American side would enable the Niagara Falls Power Company to develop between 80,000 and 100,000 horse-power.
First of all I want to call your attention to the important fact that quite aside from the merits of this proposal the state of New York was in no way invited to participate in the discussions attending this proposal; to the second important fact that the proposed weirs and structures would have to be erected on the bed of the Niagara river owned by the state of New York, and to the third important fact, that use of ten thousand cubic feet per second proposed to be withdrawn depends on the consent of the state of New York to that withdrawal and to the satisfying of the state

Preservation of Niagara Falls
of New York that if it is withdrawn the people of the state are to receive an adequate rental for this water.
In regard to the three categorical questions you asked me, I beg to advise you as follows:
(1)	In pursuance of its long standing policy the state of New York requires that its consent is prerequisite before any disposition can be made of the additional ten thousand cubic feet per second of water made available for power development by the convention.
(2)	In pursuance of the same policy of long standing the state of New York requires a charge for the use of such additional water, said charge or rental being determined in pursuance of the statutes of the state.
(3)	In your other question you ask whether the state accepts the proposal to have the work of preserving the falls, undertaken at private expense, and at the same time making available for private utilization by the Niagara Falls Power Company of the additional water to be diverted under the convention for a temporary period.
A careful reading of the proposed convention discloses the fact that the letter of the secretary of state transmitting the convention refers to a protocol to be agreed to between the United States and Canada. The protocol itself is appended to the convention and the protocol refers to the recommendations of the International Niagara Board. In other words, the three documents must be read together, and it becomes at once clear that the treaty itself is essentially an agreement to carry out a specific plan heretofore adopted. If the state of New York offers no objection to the ratification of the treaty by the Senate of the United States, the state may by inference be bound to the acceptance of the plan worked out between the International Niagara Board on the one side and the Ontario Power Commission and the Niagara Falls Power Company on the other. My easiest course as governor would have been to ask you and your colleagues in the United States Senate to oppose the ratification of the treaty as strongly as possible on the ground that the treaty ties the hands of the state of New York as to the methods by which the beautification and diversion can be arrived at, and forces the ^tate to accept the offer of the Niagara Falls Power Company.
I think that I can speak for the whole state in telling you that we want to co-operate with the federal government and the congress of the United States in every way possible to aid in the preservation of the scenic beauty of Niagara falls and the Niagara river. That is why instead of direct opposition to the ratification of the treaty, I have tried, in a spirit of co-operation, to enter into a plan by which the scenic beauty of the falls can be preserved and at the same time all of the rights of the people of the state of New York in and to their property and governmental power can be equally retained.
After a number of conferences, I am glad to say that I have been able to obtain-
It will be noted, Mr. Speaker, that he does not rely on the federal government; he goes to the power company and makes them come to time.
After a number of conferences, I am glad to say that I have been able to obtain from 
the Niagara Falls Power Company a written stipulation duly executed by it, which stipulation fully preserves the property rights and governmental authority of this state.
I might note the following facts in regard to the Niagara Falls Power Company:
(1)	It is the only private company now in a position immediately and economically to utilize the proposed experimental diversion of the additional ten thousand cubic clear in this matter.
(2)	The Niagara Falls Power Company has for a number of years been paying a rental to the state of New York for the water which it is now using.
(3)	The Niagara Falls Power Company has paid this rental to the state under protest.
The stipulation signed by the Niagara Falls Power Company agrees that if it is allowed to use for seven years the additional water obtained from this experimental diversion it will-
First: Withdraw all objections to the payment of the rental now being charged by the state for existing water, and
Secondly: Will agree to pay such equitable rental for the additional experimental supply as may be determined by the state under the water-power act, and
Thirdly:	Will recognize the necessity of
obtaining a license from the state for the use of this experimental water.
Now, Mr. Speaker, what has the Niagara board done to protect the interests of the only people who have the right to collect rentals as far as Canada is concerned? They have done absolutely nothing. You in this parliament, under this treaty, would give the Niagara board authority to divert this water without saying one word about the rentals payable to us, although that water belongs to us under the power vested in us by the province. "Oh, yes," the minister will say, " but the province of Ontario should have looked after that." Well, I am looking after it now. I do not know whether it should be our duty to go to the other people the same as the state of New York has done with respect to the power company over there and insist upon their giving us a special agreement. But the Niagara Park Commission owns the bed of the river on which these improvements are to be made. Under the treaty, through the board you have appointed, you say: We will get a permit. But what will be done suppose the permit is refused? They say: We will wait for the improvements until the permit comes. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that when the government were making this treaty they should have taken the facts of the case into consideration and not allowed the situation to get into this mess. The state of New York has taken the bull by the horns, it has gone to the private corporation

*Preservation oj Niagara Falls
and said: Do this or we will not let you make any improvements. The private corporation has done so and come to an agreement with the state. We are not in the same position.
It is the duty of this parliament to protect the park commission.

speechtext: May I ask for information-do the Hydro commission pay your board any rental for the water diverted?

subtopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF CONVENTION WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Oh yes; the Hydro, along with all the other power companies, pay a rental for the water to and through the park commission. We are the riparian owners.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I desire to refer for a moment to the Boundary Waters treaty of 1909, the treaty under which the power was originally diverted in a large quantity, and to point out to the house how the wording in relation to the water to 'be taken out is identical with the wording of the present treaty. Let me quote:
The United States may authorize and permit the diversion within the state of New York of the waters of the said river above the falls of Niagara for power purposes not exceeding in the aggregate a daily diversion at the rate of twenty thousand cubic feet of water per second.
I should like to ask either the Minister of the Interior or the Prime Minister what that means. I take it to mean that at no time during each day can you use more than twenty thousand cubic feet of water per second. That is how it reads. The new treaty provision is in identically the same words, only that an additional ten thousand cubic feet per second may be diverted. In the interpretation of the treaty usually the courts are resorted to to elucidate or explain what may be in doubt; but in this Case we have a board that does this for us. I do not think they ever had the authority but they are doing it, and I want to call the attention of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) to the fact that at the present time in the Niagara river, under the clause that provides for 56,000 cubic feet per second, 20,000 for them and 36,000 for us, more water is being taken than they have a right to receive. This board is allowing what they call a leeway or swing of 20 per cent, and they figure that, because their average over a certain period does not go beyond that therefore they are all right. But the treaty calls for 56,000 cubic feet, 36,000 on the Canadian side, and at no time must this be exceeded. One of the troubles there is accounted for partly by the fact that at times more water is ta,ken than should be. That is why I said a little while ago that the urge was power.
I do not think that this is a matter which should be left to any board to determine. The treaty is quite explicit as it stands, that so much water shall be taken and no more. Let me confirm what I said regarding the new treaty, with reference to clauses 2 and 3 wherein it is provided that the additional diversion to be permitted within the State of New York shall not exceed in the aggregate a daily diversion at the rate of 10,000 cubic feet of water per second. The same applies to Canada.
Another question that arises is this. The Prime Minister says, "This water is being taken during the winter season at a time when tourists cannot see it." Let me say to the Prime Minister and to the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) as well, who is responsible for the treaty, that they are taking that water at the time when it is lowest. And there are thousands of visitors there. Perhaps they do not know that. But it is a fact that between the very dates when they propose to take the extra water the water is then at its lowest in lake Erie. They say, of course, that this is during the period when there is no tourist traffic, when the tourists will not be able to notice the diminution in the water. But, I repeat, they are taking that extra water at a time when the falls can least afford to have it taken. In clause 1, on page 3, it is provided that additional diversions shall be permitted only within the period beginning each year on the 1st day of October and ending on the 31st day of March of the following year, both dates inclusive. Well, as I have pointed out, the period within these very dates mentioned here is the period of low water, and that is the time they expect to take the extra water. And they camouflage the whole situation by declaring that this is the time when tourists cannot see the water; if there is any shortage of water, they claim, people will not be there to notice it.
The Prime Minister has said, and the Minister of the Interior also will say, that this board has great power. They will tell us, "We can stop it at any time we see fit." I ask the house this question:	Is it a good
policy to allow private individuals, private corporations to go on and do extensive work and then tell this house that they will be stopped before they have a chance to get back their capital investment? That does not sound very good to me. The very fact that you allow private corporations to invest their money implies that there will be always the urge on their part to seek to get back their money. This enterprise should have been undertaken by the federal authorities on

Preservation of Niagara Falls [DOT]
both sides of the river so that they could be independent of any private or semi-private corporation.
Now just a word or two with regard to the remedial works. I would invite attention to page 25 of the document giving the map of the falls; there you will see an airplane picture of the falls. In two places in the river submerged weirs have been put in. Now the beauty of the falls is partly in the rapids above the falls. This picture shows the rapids all in white water, and if you glance at the Canadian side of the picture you will see in two places the effect of the submerged weirs, over a large area. Wherever the weirs are put in, you have perfectly smooth water, and I for one am very dubious about putting in submerged weirs as a means of producing a good scenic effect. The beauty of that river lies in the broken water, and where you have a submerged weir, with water smoothly flowing over it, you have not that effect.
The park commission have had this matter under consideration for the last twenty years. They made the suggestion that some islands should be put in in place of submerged weirs. We saw the effect of the weirs and did not like it, and so we asked that this suggestion be considered. It was passed over in a few words. Let me give you the exact words of the report. They are not attributed to the park commission, but the language is so framed that we felt it constituted a statement of the case which was not in accordance with our views. On page 12 of the report this statement is made with respect to remedial works:
All the plans for remedial works hitherto suggested have contemplated replenishing the flow over the flanks of the Horseshoe fall and in the American channel and at the head of Goat island. Certain plans, including those for the construction of a curved weir across the main part of the rapids above the Horseshoe, and those for distributing the flow by numerous islands in the rapids, have had for their main object a radical reduction in the heavy flow over the central part of the Horseshoe.
So far as I know, no one else but the park commission ever mentioned islands in any report. But these gentlemen add the word "numerous". We took exception to that before it was published; we told them that we had never mentioned the word "numerous" and we asked them to withdraw that word. They had that letter from us before the report was published. They had furnished us with a proof of the report two or three days before its publication. When they found we made objection to it they suddenly withdrew it, having left it in our hands for an hour, but they dated the report three days earlier than our letter. The report was pub-
lished under date of December 14 while our letter, written to them with the proof of the report, was dated December 17, and they left the word just as it stood although we never referred to "numerous" islands. Anyone can see the effect of islands; if you look at the maps you will see islands in the river to the right of Goat island. There are three or four islands there, and certainly they look a lot better than any submerged weir, and will continue to look better.
The fact remains that this Niagara board never consulted us and never took up more than fifteen or twenty minutes of the time of our engineers during the year and a quarter they were there. I do not know the gentlemen who comprise the board, but I do know their work. Some of them are engineers, no doubt quite competent, and they view the question from a practical engineering standpoint. The park commission have something more than that to look after; we have consulted the best scenic authorities in America and have had them on the ground giving us advice. I cannot find in any of the reports or from any of the men that there is a scenic man on this board. An engineer may say, "Oh, we have a scenic man" referring to Mr. Maefarland.	I dispute that; Mr. Macfarland is a publisher and for a long time has been identified with the publishing business.
I have kept a record of Mr. Maefarland for a number of years, and here is a very strange thing. I guess in the United States they proceed as we do in Canada; here if a man wishes to abolish the senate he is appointed to the senate, and as soon as he receives his appointment he changes his mind about abolishing it. This gentleman for many years hammered the board for certain things they were doing and for taking water out of the Niagara. I have some of his work here, and when it was proposed to take 56,000 cubic feet from the river he went almost crazy. He even published pictures of Niagara falls running dry about fifteen or twenty years ago, with 56,000 cubic feet taken from it, but after being appointed to the board this same gentleman changed his mind and is now willing to take 20.000 cubic feet more from the river when there is less water going over than before. That is pretty good, I would say. Let me refer to just one of his articles, published when he belonged to the American Civic Association. It is headed:
The Impending Destruction of Niagara Falls. This is dated 1905, when the agitation was going on, and when it was intended to take

Preservation ol Niagara Falls
56,000	cubic feet from the falls. The article proceeds:
Ten power-developing companies (four American and six Canadian) now have authority to utilize 35i per cent (1,339,500 horse-power) of the effective power of the falls. . . .
If even half the authorized amount of water is withdrawn above the cataract, the American rapids will be entirely bare of water	
You can see that this gentleman was not very much of a prophet; he did not see what was going to take place and certainly he could not have believed his statements of a few years ago when he can consent to the withdrawal of an additional 20,000 cubic feet from the falls. I have a whole book full of material having to do with this gentleman; he is a publisher, and is no more entitled to have the word " scenic " attached to him than I am, and perhaps not so much. So far as I am concerned I have lived with this proposition for some twenty years during which I have been on the board, and we have been grappling with it all the time. He has been fighting it in the United States, but now he turns around and comes out in favour of the diversion of more water.
I started out by saying, Mr. Speaker, that the whole thing was a power proposition, and I ask that the government of Canada go slow and be very careful in what they do at Niagara. Personally I believe something can be done; whether or not you are on the right track I do not know, but as I have already said you have no right to ask a private corporation to spend their money on a proposition of this kind, because they must get that money back. That is the point I want to convey; they must get that money back and the impulse which will come to any one in charge is to give them a chance to do so, which is not in the best interests of scenic Niagara.

speakeroldname: Hon. CHARLES STEWART (Minister of the Interior):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was greatly interested in the statement made by the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Chaplin) with respect to the remedial works proposed to be placed in the Niagara river to preserve the scenic qualities of the falls, as well as to provide for a temporary diversion of 20,000 cubic feet divided equally between the two countries. I did intend to give a somewhat lengthy and detailed explanation of the whole matter, but in view of what has been said by the Prime Minister, supplemented by the remarks of the two hon. gentlemen who have just spoken, I think I oan dispense with that.
In 1922, when I became Minister of the Interior, one of the first questions presented to me was this problem of the preservation
of the falls. My hon. friends have stated that it has been a matter of controversy for years, and I think wisely so, from my own observations and speaking from what I have been able to observe at Niagara falls. Neither the hon. member for Lincoln nor the other speaker will deny that gradually, year by year, the concentration of the flowage there is getting through the Horseshoe and that there is not the same recession on the other parts of the crest of the falls. So much is that the fact that the water has practically ceased to flow next to Goat island, and for a large part of the year the whole crest line is exposed for a considerable distance from Goat island towards the Horseshoe. Naturally this has caused some concern.
Here and now I want to say that no one regrets it more than I do if the board appointed by the provincial government of Ontario for the purpose of preserving the park and the scenic qualities of the falls was not fully consulted and presented with every detail ascertained by the engineers of both governments. First let me say that no one can negotiate a treaty but the federal government at Ottawa and the federal government at Washington. If there is to be any change, of necessity these two governments must take the responsibility of making the treaty, and I do say that the first duty of a minister, the advisor of the federal government, is to keep himself fully in touch with the provincial governments affected. It is needless for me to say that the provincial government of Ontario would be vitally affected by any change which might take place in connection with this matter. We took the precaution of keeping very closely in touch with them and also had the advice of the Hydro engineers during the whole of this investigation. They played as large a part in arriving at the conclusion as did our engineers. In addition, there was complete collaboration with the American engineers before any definite program was laid dawn as to the purpose for which the board was created. Early in 1923 we directed our attention to the very matter which my hon. friend complains about, namely, that we were rapidly approaching a period when the power interests on both sides of the river would have full utilization of the 56,000 cubic feet per second provided for in the former treaty. We had not taken the precaution of ascertaining how much water was being used on our side, so we immediately set about that task and informed ourselves as to the flowage passing through these plants, and obtained full data on that particular question. In 1923 or 1924 -I am not exactly sure of my date-I visited

Preservation of Niagara Falls
Niagara Falls and saw a panorama which had been made up-no doubt my hon. friend has seen the same thing-by the American engineers. The water was turned on this model and showed the proposed improvements in order that, we might see just what the effect would be.

speechtext: Will the minister state on what ground the government of Canada thought they could deal with this matter? Was it a question of the peace, order and good government of the Dominion, or in what way did the Dominion profess to deal with it?

subtopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF CONVENTION WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext: It is the only way it could be dealt with; it certainly could not be dealt with by the Ontario government.

subtopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF CONVENTION WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext: Perhaps I have not made myself clear. You are dealing with a province in a matter that does not involve any question of a navigable stream, and I want to know under what Dominion jurisdiction the minister acted.

subtopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF CONVENTION WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext: I do not consider it necessary to cite any particular statute or clause giving us authority. Having the assurance of the premier of Ontario, and of the manager of the Hydro that this treaty was entirely satisfactory, before we attempted to negotiate the treaty, I thought I was on safe ground in advising the government.

speechtext: Has the government any binding form of consent or authority from the provincial government to deal with the lands in question, the river bed and that sort of thing? I would be very glad if the minister would say just how that consent came about.

subtopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF CONVENTION WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Remedial
works in question are to be undertaken by the Hydro, who are parties to the treaty and who, I assume, are the creation of the

Preservation of Niagara Falls
provincial government and have that government behind them. I say to my hon. friend that the authority which oreated his board is in agreement about these remedial works proposed by the treaty.

speechtext: By letter, resolution, order in council or what?

subtopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF CONVENTION WITH UNITED STATES

subtopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF CONVENTION WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext:
I do not have it in my possession at this minute, but I will obtain it later on.
I do not think my hon. friend, even with his thirty years' experience, is competent to say what engineering works are necessary to bring about this desirable result. These works are the result of the best judgment of a corps of engineers most of whom are of outstanding ability. Doctor Camsell is not an engineer but he was placed on .this board by this government because of the fact that erosion played a very important part in arriving at a decision as to what measures should be taken to remedy the apparent evil on the crest line of the falls. What the engineers hoped to do-I am discussing this purely as a layrnah-is to spread the water more evenly over the crest of the falls and stop the divergence into the Horseshoe falls which is receding at a much more rapid rate than the full crest line. Eventually, if it is not stopped, it will destroy the scenic beauty of the falls. I do not think that will be contradicted.
Part of the improvement is the proper distribution of flowage, so that the flow will cover the whole crest of the falls. They state in the report, that that is what they believe will happen when these remedial works are completed. My hon. friend has made a great deal of the fact that they have stated in the report that the increased flowage will occur only during the non-tourist season and, as he points out, at the low flowage period of the river itself, and that therefore it will do no harm. What I want to point out to my hon. friend in addition to that and what I think he has missed, is that they state most emphatically that, in regard to the scenic effect and the lighting effect, the full covering of the crest line of the falls will come as a result of these works at every period of the year.

subtopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF CONVENTION WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext: I never disputed that. I do not dispute it now. I admit it.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
subtopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF CONVENTION WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext:
I am satisfied if my hon. friend admits that; that is conclusive, and I wish to present the case
to the house as I get it from the report of the engineers. Competent engineers on both sides have made a careful study of this matter; they have investigated all the proposals that were made to them as being necessary for the protection of the scenic quality of the falls. They have taken the precaution to recommend that this diversion shall continue only for a period of seven years. During that period they have stated that the board will continue carefully to watch the improvement and ascertain whether further remedial works than those proposed will be necessary.

speechtext:
What has the minister
to say about this work being done by private enterprise on the one side?

subtopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF CONVENTION WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext: I was coming to that. If my hon. friend's contention was correct that it was entirely private enterprise, there might be something in it, because I am willing to admit there is something in the argument of my hon. friend that, if it is found that these works are not sufficient for the purpose for which they are desired or that, by their installation and by the diversion of additional water, the falls will suffer, then because private capital has been put in, we would be compelled to continue the work for the period of seven years. My reply to that is that it will be at least three years or a fair proportion of three years out of the seven before these works are fully completed. As regards the Canadian side of the improvement I was attracted to it owing to the very fact that my hon. friend has mentioned, namely, that there is a scarcity of power, but I would require to be assured that the abstraction will not in any way affect the scenic qualities of the falls themselves. I have that assurance. My hon. friend doubts that, but I am giving him the word, as I have said, of a corps of competent engineers, and the Ontario government, who are the creators of and who own the Hydro system, are going to provide one-half of the cost of the installation.

subtopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF CONVENTION WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext:
My hon.
friend will admit that it is always stated that it is a provincial institution. It may be the municipalities, but it is the people of the province of Ontario-

speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF CONVENTION WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext:
-who constitute one of the consenting parties to this

Preservation oj Niagara Falls
agreement. The members of the house may not agree that the people of Ontario represented by their government, knew what they were doing, but I say that they knew every detail, both of the work itself with respect to the suggested development and of the cost. Indeed the cost was arrived at by collaborating with their own engineers so that what I have to say as a representative of the federal government is that, knowing these facts, I, with full confidence, recommended that the Dominion government join with the United States government in the ratification of the treaty.

speechtext:
I have only this to say in regard to
the seven-year period, that my experience with respect to government undertakings of that kind has not been very good. I was engaged at one time on behalf of a former government of this country in connection with an application by a United States corporation known as the Aluminum Company of America, to divert temporarily a large flowage of water from the river St. Lawrence to the Long Sault rapids. The case occupied about ten days in the city of Montreal. It was held by the International Joint Commission that the application was launched as a war measure; the additional power was required by the aluminum company at their works in the state of New York to produce aluminum war goods. It had the sanction of the President of the United States. An arrangement was ordered by the International Joint commission to give the aluminum company a special diversion of water from the St. Lawrence river for the purpose of their works. They were tMr. C. A. Stewart.]
to construct weirs, dams and the like for a period of five years after which the dams were to be taken out and the water restored to its natural flow. But what happened? The arrangement was subsequently made a permanent one. They have this diversion of water and they are using it to-day. I am afraid that what happened in that case is very likely to happen in the present case.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
subtopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF CONVENTION WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext:
The mere
fact that they got the five-year period did not in any way entitle them to receive a continuation of their contract.

But they got it and the argument used in that case will be the argument used in this: there is the dam; there is the expenditure; why allow this water to run to waste? At the end of the seven-year period it will be said:	This flow of 10,000
cubic feet on each side was to be utilized for power purposes; it has been so utilized for seven years; why not let it be used in the future? This looks like a permanent diversion of 10,000 cubic feet of water on each side of the river. Speaking for myself, and for myself alone, as the Dominion government seems to be satisfied with the arrangement, and as the government of the province of Ontario seems to be satisfied with it, notwithstanding that personally I am doubtful as to the propriety of the arrangement, I am willing to let it go.

subtopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF CONVENTION WITH UNITED STATES
