Preservation of Niagara Falls

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
subtopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF CONVENTION WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext: If my hon. friend is determined not to accept the judgment of competent engineers, then I have nothing more to say.

subtopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF CONVENTION WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext:
I just wish to say a few words on this matter.
I do not feel myself capable of entering into the controversy, but I have listened with a great deal of interest, as all hon. members no doubt have done, to the speeches that have been made on this question by the Prime Minister, the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) and by my hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr. Chaplin), because if there is a beauty spot in all Canada which should be preserved for our children and their children, it is Niagara falls. Away back in the days of the old French explorers, we have references to its great beauty, even ;by men most of whose time was taken up fighting the Indians. I remember reading just the other day a statement by one of the old explorers, Hennepin, who was the first to point out the beauties of Niagara falls, and from that time on to this day, Niagara falls has been one of the scenic wonders of the world. I do not know anybody who has visted the falls on a number of occasions who has not come away each time with a greater appreciation of its sublimity than he had on the previous visit. Therefore I say that anything that can be done to preserve the beauty of the falls should be done.
The hon. member for Lincoln is a member of that board, representing the province of Ontario, whose sole duty it is to preserve the scenic beauty of Niagara falls. The members of that board have no financial interest in the matter whatever. I believe I am correct in saying that they have been working on the board many years without cost to the province of Ontario, and their whole efforts have been to preserve its beauty for the province and the Dominion generally.
There has been a dispute apparently here this afternoon. The hon. member for Lincoln points out that while submerged weirs may bring about a spreading of the water, they do not result in as beautiful an effect as an island or a series of islands would. The point I wish to make is that as there is some dispute as to the results to be obtained from the standpoint of beauty by the construction of these proposed remedial works, as there is some doubt as to their effectiveness in the minds of this board which has been charged with the preservation of the beauty of the falls for many years, on behalf of the province of Ontario and Canada generally, I think
this whole treaty should be held up temporarily, at least, until further consideration can be given to it. It seems to me extraordinary-I am not saying this in a critical spirit, because I suppose it was an oversight- that the board appointed by this government should not have consulted the one body in Canada which has been giving its time and its energies to preserve this magnificent and sublime scene in all its beauty for the people of this country, and, indeed, the whole world, and if for no other reason, I think the whole matter should be held up for further consideration. We all know that there has been a gradual process of erosion going on at the apex of Horseshoe falls. The Prime Minister said this afternoon that it amounted to 3.7 feet per annum, and that some remedial works are necessary to preserve the scenic beauty of the falls. It has been suggested by my hon. friend from Lincoln, and after listening to this whole debate very carefully I would say, properly suggested, that this whole scheme is a power scheme, and therefore I do think that the one body in Canada that is particularly interested in Niagara falls from the standpoint of beauty should have been consulted. They should have been given an opportunity to discuss this whole question with the Canadian board, and with the American board, perhaps, and should have been given the opportunity to present their conclusions after all these years of study.
There is another reason why I think this matter should be held over. I have been told-I heard it stated yesterday-that the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), who has been called out of the city by reason of the illness of a relative, wished to take part in this discussion. For that reason also I should like to see this question held over. After all, I do not think there is any great hurry. I do not think the treaty has been ratified by the American senate, and in this materialistic age I do not think there is any need for us to hurry simply because there may be a desire to develop more power by some company or companies. We should not be hurried by such a consideration in a matter of this kind. I suggest with due respect to the Prime Minister that he hold over the 'consideration of this treaty for two or three weeks, so that this commission of which my hon. friend from Lincoln is a member, and of which all of us who have given any thought to the matter are so proud, because of the work they have done in beautifying the parks adjoining the falls, may be given an opportunity to consult with the new board that has been appointed.

Preservation oj Niagara Falls

subtopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF CONVENTION WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext:
My friend who has just sat down (Mr. Manion) has touched upon a point which I think is very well worthy of consideration by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), and it is a point upon which I venture to ask a question. I would like to know very definitely what form the consent of the province of Ontario took. Who instituted this inquiry, and how closely has the province of Ontario kept in touch with the work of the engineers? It. seems to me extraordinary that the province of Ontario, if it were keeping closely in touch with the engineers, would neglect to consult the body of all bodies which has had to do, not with electric power, but with the scenic beauty of the falls. That has been professedly the first consideration, and it is [DOT] therefore scarcely understandable that the province of Ontario should have neglected to consult the body which has scenic beauty in its care, rather than the development of power. If the minister will consider the circumstances of the appointment of this board, he first of all had the nucleus of the board in the presence of two gentlemen who had to do with overlooking the diversion of water provided for under the treaty of 1909. They are more or less power engineers; at least, I judge that they had to do with the diversion of water for power purposes. To this nucleus there were added two other engineers, but the board is primarily a power board. By whom was it instructed, and on whose letter is that board working? On the letter of two power companies, people primarily interested in power, the Hydro-Electric Power Commission of Ontario, and some power company on the other side of the river. So that you have loaded against you, so to speak, on the power side as against the scenic side, the personnel of the board, as well as those who are advising the board. When the hon. member for Lincoln discussed the question of submerged weirs, as opposed to "weirs," rising above the surface in the form of an island, or however they may be built, he was speaking of something which he has had every opportunity to study thoroughly. Those weirs will be left. The power people may fall down with respect to the scenic aspect, but you may be quite sure that when they finish putting in the weirs, those weirs will be amply sufficient to divert the water necessary under their plans, that is, ten thousand cubic feet per second. So I would suggest to the minister that he keep a very close eye on the development as it affects the scenic feature of the falls. After all, I think that is what we here are most interested in. We get only tbn 
thousand cubic feet per second as against the ten thousand allowed the United States. The original proportion was as 36 to 20. Why are we not getting the same proportion of the additional diversion instead of only one-half?
I agree with the member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) that after the very careful presentation by the member for Lincoln, who knows- the situation so thoroughly, and having in view that the chief abject of this house is the preservation of the scenic beauty of the falls and not the development of power, more time might be given for the consideration of this question.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF CONVENTION WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext: May I say, Mr. Speaker-

subtopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF CONVENTION WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext: Is the Prime Minister going to close the debate?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF CONVENTION WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext:
No, that is exactly what I am not going to do, but I wish to make reference to the request that the debate be adjourned tall the hon. leader of the opposition returns. May I say that when I learned the hon. leader of the opposition unfortunately was .to be called away, I crossed the floor and asked him if there was anything on the order paper which he would wish to have held1 over until he returned, because if so I should be pleased to endeavour to see that his wishes were met. The hon. leader of the opposition assured me to the contrary, and advised that the government proceed with the orders exactly as we might wish. That is the reason why we are proceeding to-day with this resolution. Inasmuch, however, as it has been suggested that the resolution be held over until the leader of the opposition returns, I am only too happy to accept the suggestion. It is quite possible that .the leader of the opposition may not have thought of mentioning his wishes to me, but afterwards may have mentioned to others that he would like to speak on the resolution.
I might add, Mr. Speaker, that the federal government acts of necessity as the government which has to do with the negotiation of treaties with a foreign country in matters of national concern. In taking up this matter, however, the federal government has had in mind primarily the province of Ontario and its special interest in addition to that of the entire Dominion in the scenic beauties of Niagara falls. If in Ontario the provincial authorities, who have been closely in touch with this matteT throughout, and to whom it is of more concern than it is to the authori-

C.N.R-Purchase oj Railways
ties of any other province, do not wish to have the treaty proceeded with, the government certainly will not press the matter further the next time the treaty is under discussion.

subtopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF CONVENTION WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext: 'May I correct an impression that I gave the house? I had no authority to speak for the leader of the opposition, but I heard him express his intention when this matter came up to take part in the discussion. I quite agree with the Prime Minister that the leader of the opposition might easily have overlooked this. But I think an adjournment of the debate would serve two purposes; it would give him an opportunity to take whatever part in the debate he may think adv'sable, and, more important still, it would give time for reconsideration of the whole proposition.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF CONVENTION WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext: I do not wish it to ibe understood, Mr. Speaker, that the government has any doubt in its mind in regard to the matter. But seeing that the province of Ontario is primarily involved, and that the government has relied upon the engineers of the Ontario government to keep advised the Ontario government as well as the agencies of that government, I am quite agreeable, in view of my hon. friend's request, to have the debate adjourned.

Hon. P. J. A. CARDIN (Minister of Marine and Fisheries) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to authorize a loan to the harbour commissioners of Vancouver in an amount not exceeding $10,000,000 to carry on the construction of terminal _ facilities, upon approval by the governor in council of detailed plans, specifications _ and estimates for such works, and the deposit of debentures of the corporation to cover said loan.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Johnston in the chair.

This resolution provides for the introduction of a bill to authorize an advance of $10,000,000 to the harbour commissioners of Vancouver. The representations made to me by the commissioners are that they need this sum of money for the following purposes:	First, for the redemption of
commissioners' mortgage notes issued for the balance of the purchase price of the property known as the Hastings mill, the amount of these notes being $1,950,000; secondly, to provide for developmental work on the above property in the way of docks and terminal facilities; and, thirdly, for needed extensions to the elevator facilities. This probably will be for financing only; these, facilities will likely be leased in advance for an amount covering interest and sinking fund.
There is no doubt that the harbour of Vancouver is in need of further development. Business has been increasing there rapidly, last year having been an exceptionally good year in the administration of the harbour. The receipts of the harbour of Vancouver, amounting in 1924 to $1,870,000 totalled in 1928, $2,057,739. The expenditure has been a little less than it was in 1924. In 1924 the expenditure was $1,741,000 and in 1928, $1,682,000. So that after paying interest on the money advanced by the government to the commissioners and providing for the sinking fund the commission is left with a very substantial surplus. It is quite clear, therefore, that the business of the port has been very good. And it is contended that the facilities asked for will help materially in still further increasing that business.
There are certain details which I have asked the commissioners to furnish me with before we get through with the bill, and under the circumstances I would ask the committee, if

Three Rivera Harbour Commission

I presume the minister will be able to give information in the way of an official statement with regard to the terminal elevator.

speechtext:
The harbour of Three
Rivers is not so important as the harbour with which we dealt last, but this port is very useful to the city of Three Rivers and also to the adjoining communities. As hon. gentlemen know, the city of Three Rivers is an important centre for the production of paper and is also one of the most important cities in the province of Quebec from an industrial point of view. During past years expenditures have been made on this harbour through the Department of Public Works; expensive wharves have been built and a certain amount of dredging carried on. In view of the request from the commissioners for an advance of $2,000,000 to place them on an equal footing with other harbour commissions, the government have decided to stop the expenditures formerly made through the Department of Public Works, and this money is to provide for necessary developments and increased facilities.
The port of Three Rivers is largely used for the importation of coal necessary in the production of pulp and paper, and it might be interesting to know the amout of business done by this port in the past. I have not the complete figures, 'but during the year 1924 the total receipts were about $39,000 and during 1928 they increased to roughly $74,000, so that in four years the receipts have practically doubled. In 1924 the expenditures amounted to about $24,000 and in 1928 to $34,000, in

Three Rivers Harbour Commission
round! figures, so after providing for their expenditures and meeting their indebtedness the commissioners are left with a relatively large surplus.
Might I ask the capital expenditure involved for the year 1928?

Have they paid the
interest on all these debentures?
Yes; the interest is included in the expenditures I have mentioned.

Just for the sake of information I would like to ask the minister with reference to the port of Three Rivers, which we all recognize as a very important industrial city, whether it is not a fact that the principal users of the port are the big paper companies. If that is so, why do they not supply their own facilities, as they do elsewhere? Then I would like to know from the minister just what are the principal imports and exports. He has said that coal is the principal import; naturally that is used by the pulp and 'paper mills of the Three Rivers district. Then I understand that there are also very substantial imports of puLpwood; for instance, in recent years, a substantial quantity of pulpwood has been shipped by the International Paper Company from the Miramichi district in New Brunswick to Three Rivers. Why is it that these paper companies, which are so prosperous, do not supply their own port facilities? Why do they ask the government to do this work when in other parts of Canada the big manufacturing establishments have to do it themselves? I would like to know from the minister also what are the principal exports; if they are paper products from the mills located in that district why should not these companies supply their own facilities? I am not saying the policy is wrong, but I am merely asking for the sake of information.

It is true that the main
imports are coal and pulpwood and the exports are mainly paper products, but when these big companies use the facilities they pay the dues. If they had their own wharves they would use them and the public would not have the advantage of such facilities. For instance, there is a steel plant at Three Rivers, and if my hon. friend's suggestion were [Mr. Cardin.1
adopted they could not use these facilities. I see nothing wrong in the fact that most of the facilities are used by the paper companies provided they pay for them, as they do. They are not getting any special privileges; they pay for the use of the wharves and at the same time these facilities are available to other concerns in the locality.

I am not suggesting there is anything wrong about it; the minister must not understand that from my remarks. This is a matter of public policy which I presume has been well studied, and if all the other ports of Canada were doing the business industrially, that they are doing at Three Rivers I should be only too glad. As a matter of fact, however, is it not true that about ninety per cent of the total imports and exports are occasioned by these'big paper companies who are supplied with these facilities at the public expense? It is true that they pay the charges, but why should Canada make these capital expenditures for large corporations who are able to take care of themselves?

At the moment I would
not be ready to admit that ninety per cent, eighty per cent or even seventy-five per cent of the business of the port is done by these mills. Hon. members will realize that Three Rivers, with a population of 35,000 itself and more than that in the surrounding district, i3 in need of harbour facilities, and the harbour is used not only by the industries of Three Rivers but also by those in the surrounding districts such as the towns of Grand-Mere and Shawinigan. These two towns are quite important, and the port serves not only the north shore of the St. Lawrence but the south shore as well. A ferry runs from the south shore to Three Rivers. The south shore of the St. Lawrence will benefit through the facilities provided for the export of agricultural products. I think the facilities in the harbour are necessary for the general good of the community, outside of the use which will be made of them by the large power companies.
Will the minister give us the value of the agricultural exports through the port of Three Rivers?

The minister stated, I
think, that the total income for 1928 was $74,000, while the expenditure was $34,000, leaving a surplus of $40,000. It is proposed to expend $2,000,000, and if the rate of interest on the bonds is put at 5 per cent it means an interest charge of over $100,000. I suggest that on the second reading of this 'bill the min-

Chicoutimi Harbour Commission
ister have the information available which will show how that extra $100,000 is to be obtained from the traffic going through that port. Can the minister give any information as to the total expenditures made prior to the time the commission took over this harbour, and whether the commission has been charged up with those expenditures, the same as was done with Quebec?

I have not that information, but I will get it and present it on the second
reading.

I want to know if we
are treating this port the same as Quebec, or whether some new arrangement should be made for Quebec.

commissioners.

Horn. P. J. A. CARDIN (Minister of Marine and Fisheries) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to authorize a loan to the harbour commissioners of Chicoutimi in an amount not exceeding $2,000,000 to carry on the construction of terminal facilities, upon approval by the governor in council of detailed plans, specifications and estimates for such works, and the deposit of debentures of the corporation to cover said loan.
He said:	In this case we are dealing with
a locality which is practically new in the field of industry. Chicoutimi is situated at the head of the Saguenay river, about seventy miles north of the St. Lawrence. That river is the discharge of lake St. John which is a very large reservoir of water and has been used lately for the development of important water-powers. As a result of this development of Jake St. John, ten or fifteen industries have been established in that locality. In the region of that lake about 1,500,000 horse-power will be developed. No one can doubt the importance of that locality from an industrial point of view when this power development is finally completed. At the present time a large amount of power is being developed and is ready for the market. Practically the whole of the operations of the American Aluminum Company are to be carried on at that place.
Eight or ten years ago the town of Chicoutimi had a population of about 7,000, but 78594-3li
to-day there is a population of about 15,000, and there are over 60,000 people in the surrounding district. At present the only harbour facilities at this point consists of a wharf about 500 feet long. A large amount of coal is imported for the use of the mills and other plants established in the vicinity of lake St. John and Chicoutimi. In 1925, even with the poor facilities, nearly 115,000 tons of goods went through the port of Chicoutimi, and also a large amount of dressed lumber. At the present time there are no facilities to- deal with the coal which is required for the different industries established at Chicoutimi, and I think the prospects of the future traffic through this port completely justify the advance of money proposed.
I am not in position to state definitely that this commission will be in position to pay the first year's interest on the advance, but we must remember that if we had not proceeded through the incorporation of a commission, large expenditures would have had to be made through the Department of Public Works. Every hon. gentleman in this committee knows of places where money has been advanced through the Department of Public Works and upon which the government will receive no interest. But, judging from the reports and representations made to me and taking cognizance of the situation there, I sincerely expect that this port is going to meet its responsibilities and that in the course of a few years it will meet its obligations. I repeat: we must do something; there is no escape from that. When we have all these industries located in the river, with that amount of power being developed there and important industries established there, there is no doubt that the government would be forced one way or another to make expenditures to provide facilities in that port.
Is this a company?
No, it is not a company at all.
There have been no expenditures prior to the present time by the harbour commission?
Yes, last year parliament under a bill voted a sum of $500,000, and with that money the commissioners started enlarging the wharf which existed at that time ir the harbour of Chicoutimi.
Are they making charges at the present time for service?

Yes, last year they collected the sum of $18,000 in connection with their facilities.
484	COMMONS
Divorce Cowl-Mr. Bell (Hamilton)
Why does the minister not make this a gift instead of a loan? He does not expect to receive any interest from it.
I certainly expect a return on it and there is justification for my expectation. The town is going to grow very rapidly.
Has the minister any better expectations in this case than in that of Quebec?

The town is not as important as Quebec is now, but a few years from now I am sure it will have grown to such importance that we shall get all the returns we need to meet the interest charges and sinking fund in connection with the amount we are lending them.
That is a speculation.
Far better than the Toronto terminals.	[DOT]
How long will it be before this $2,000,000 will be spent?
I want to make it a gift.
We fear the Greeks even bearing gifts.

The bill which will be introduced provides that before starting work they have to submit a plain to the engineers of the Department of Marine and Fisheries and the plan has to be approved before the loan which has been authorized is spent.
The question I asked was how long it would be before the $2,000,000 would be spent? Would it be one year or two years?

More than two years.

The house resumed from February 22 consideration of the motion of Mr. Woodsworth for the second reading of Bill No. 38, to provide in the province of Ontario for the dissolution and annulment of marriage.

Mr. Speaker. I desire to associate myself with the remarks that have already been made in favour of this bill by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth), and the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa). I think it must have furnished to the house a striking commentary on the situation which has been created, and which has called for the introduction of this legislation, to find a bill of this nature introduced by a member from the province of Manitoba and endorsed by a member from the province of Quebec.
My hon. friend the member for Labelle the other night seemed to feel that the situation called for some remarks upon the question of provincial rights, and the assertion of provincial rights in this house. It is not in that spirit that I am approaching the discussion of the bill to-night. Rather I take it that both the hon. gentlemen who have spoken on the subject so far have addressed themselves to it mainly because, although themselves not residents of the province of Ontario, they felt that it deals with a very important question of right and wrong, and it is upon that basis that I desire to address to the house such remarks as now occur to' me.
It has already been stated that there is practically no issue here as to the principle of divorce, that the method is the only question which is before the house for consideration. I can readily understand how many persons who are conscientiously opposed to the idea of divorce might state to the house that they felt constrained, upon principle, to oppose the bill in the hope that thereby they would put an end to something which they regard a.s an unmixed evil. But, sir, we know from the record that we have before us, and from the situation in which we find ourselves to-day, that there is no such thing as doing away with divorce, and that the only question before the house now is whether divorce shall be dealt with to the best advantage, or dealt with in a less satisfactory manner.
There are two or three points in connection with this bill that I desire to present for the consideration of the house. It has been already pointed out by my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre that every year finds a largely increasing number of these applications, and that it has been recently found impossible for the senate of the parliament of Canada to deal with all the applications that come before it in the course of a single session; so much so that, as we already know, this year there has been formed, or is in

Divorce Court-Mr. Bell (Hamilton)
process of formation, a second divorce committee of the senate. Judging by the rate at which these applications have been increasing in the last few years, we shall very shortly find ourselves confronted with the necessity, df the senate is to continue to deal with these measures, of creating not simply one additional committee but two or three or four additional committees. It was the case,
I believe, last year-I stand subject to correction if I am wrong-that although a large number of applications had been received, and although the divorce committee of the senate addressed themselves with great earnestness to the problem of dealing with those applications and followed them up with the utmost industry, even then it was not possible during the period of the session to deal with all the applications that came before the senate. So we had the unfortunate anomaly at the conclusion of the session, that decrees were granted to a number of people who had cases which upon being tested were found to be good, while on the other hand a large number of people who had cases presumably just as good and just as worthy of the decree of the divorce committee were forced into the position of not having their petitions decided upon simply because there was no time to deal with them. Surely we cannot say that the decision of the senate and of this house is being given with equality to all, as long as the test of relief-assuming that the applicants are entitled to relief at all- shall be, not the justice of their cause but merely the possibility of the senate overtaking its work and dealing with their petitions. That, I think, sir, is a proposition which will commend itself to every member of this house.
But there is something far more serious than that. The method of granting divorce on the recommendation of the senate committee and the passing of a private bill has set up this condition in the Dominion-that the man who is fairly well-to-do, if he has a just cause, can present that cause and have it adjudicated; but the man who is poor is denied that right. Surely it should not *be possible anywhere in this country that material wealth should be the test of right or wrong. It is well known to all those whose work calls upon them to undertake the presenting of divorce applications to the senate divorce committee, that ever so often it is found that those who have a perfectly just cause, a cause founded upon honest, indisputable evidence, are nevertheless compelled to abandon that cause simply for the reason that they have not
the requisite funds to take the steps necessary to obtain a decree. The fact is that under present conditions any man or woman in this Dominion who seeks relief by way of divorce must be able to pay for the cost of the senate bill, for the cost of having that bill looked after through the senate and through this house, and muA be able also to meet the necessary expenses, which sometimes are extremely heavy, of bringing witnesses from the uttermost parts of the country to this city in order that their evidence may be heard by the committee and passed upon.
What a monstrous situation it would be that a man who, for example, had instituted suit for breach of contract should be told:	You
cannot obtain relief under the law unless you take your case to the city of Ottawa, no matter in what part of Canada you may reside. This is identically the situation in relation to divorce. The only possible way by which divorce could be made easy to people of small means would be to say that the sittings of the senate committee which is empowered to recommend the granting of a decree should be held throughout the length and breadth of the land. But we know how utterly impracticable that is. We know it is out of the question to consider it for one moment.
*So, sir, we have this situation-and it must continue unless this bill is proceeded with of people being able to say:	I may have a
just cause, I may have evidence right under my hand to entitle me to a decree of divorce, a decree which in fairness, honesty and justice I ought to be granted, but because of the fact that I am not possessed of sufficient funds to go to Ottawa and to pay the fees incidental to an application for divorce and to bear the expense of bringing witnesses to the capital, I am denied that relief which as a citizen of Canada is mine, and mine by right. Only by supporting this bill can that grievous inequality be removed. I think it is a standing reproach to this parliament and to tnis country that any citizen who has a just cause to seek divorce should be told:	You have
not the money, and therefore there is no possibility of your cause being heard. In other words, he is told: You are deprived of justice at the hands of the high court of parliament, the very highest court in the land.
It is for that reason, Mr. Speaker, that preeminent, that paramount reason, that I ally myself with my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre who, as I see it, has unearthed a very grievous wrong that ought to be remedied. And until that wrong is remedied

Divorce. Court-Mr. McMillan
this parliament cannot divest itself of the reproach that under present conditions it is granting one thing to the well-to-do, and denying that same thing to the poor.

Mr. Speaker, I feel this is a question which should be regarded from the most serious point of view. My hon. friend who has just taken his seat (Mr. Bell) has approached the question in the belief, apparently, that we are all in favour of the principle of divorce.
No, no.

Now, sir, so far as I
am concerned I must dissent from that view. Since I have had the privilege of a seat in this parliament I am at one with my hon. friend in saying that the manner in which these cases have received attention in this chamber is nothing less than a travesty. Many times I have thought of it seriously, and felt like rising to my feet in protest.
There may be hon. members present who are in favour of the principle of divorce. I have always held the opinion, and I am to-day more strongly than ever of the view, that marriage is a sacred union. Marriage is the key to the home: the home is the bulwark of society and of the nation. We talk of the greatness of our country, of our wealth, of our wonderful natural resources, but we should never forget that the greatest asset of a nation is the integrity of its people. The character and condition of the people is either the greatest asset or it is the most detestable scourge of a country. Therefore that thought brings me back at once to our homes and the home life of our people. In the mad rush and struggle for wealth and property and material possessions, which in this country is everywhere apparent, the higher and better things which go to build up the home and build up humanity should not be neglected. As I have said, the home is the bulwark of the nation. History records the fact that it has always been so, and it will continue to be so until the end of time. Go back into history and study it. Study, if you will, that old volume of the sacred law. What does it tell us? Among all its wonderful words of wisdom and of admonition to the human race, it tells us that in mere wealth, in mere sordid wealth and outward splendour, old Babylon had no rivals in ancient times. But her fatal weakness was that she put no real estimate upon true manhood. As a consequence, her gorgeous palaces and hanging gardens became the abode of selfishness and sensuality, with the result, as we now read, that 
over that spurious greatness rests the stillness of the desert, the gloom of an eternal night. It was in view of all this that Scotland's immortal bard tells us in The Cottar's Saturday Night:
How he, "who lone in Patinos banished,
Saw in the sun a mighty angel stand,
And heard great, Bab'lon's doom pronounc'd by Heaven's command.
What of Greece? Ancient Greece was not a large country-her chief city, Athens-less populous than New York. Her people were great in art, great in philosophy, great in wisdom and great even in a certain kind of patriotism. But the fatal weakness of the people of Greece was that they bad no real, true family life. Their public men were corrupt in their habits, loose in their morals, and their women, even the most accomplished, were unchaste. As a consequence, the fate of Greece was inevitable; and her fall was even more rapid than her rise.
What of ancient Rome? Read Gibbon's decline and fall of the Roman empire: we are told that that fall was due to the general corruption of the people and their engrossing love of pleasure and idleness. So long as the nobility of Rome considered it an honour to labour with their hands, so long as they continued to recognize the dignity of honest labour, Rome continued to flourish. We read of the time when the land was tilled in those days even by generals; as they left the field of battle they returned triumphant to the plough. But when the ruling classes of Rome began to live so luxuriously and so extravagantly that they considered honest labour as beneath their dignity, and as fit only for the engagement of serfs and slaves, from that day onwards dates the decay and downfall of the Roman empire.
Coming to the middle ages, we have no doubt all read of the time when Spain was the mightiest of European powers. The discoveries of Columbus had added to her possessions the new world of the west. The conquests of Cortez and Pizarro had poured into its treasury the riches of Mexico and of Peru. Its galleons brought the gold, the jewels and the ingots of silver to the harbour of Cadiz, while at the same time Philip was endeavouring to add to his possessions some of the fairest and wealthiest portions of western continental Europe. What were the means by which Spain was able to hold her people in subjection? It was through the terror of the Inquisition and the power of the stake and the sword. By such means a nation could never continue to flourish, and that country

Divorce Court-Mr. Arthurs
having been humbled and broken through the defeat of the Armada, her greatness soon dwindled away.
Let us come still nearer to our own time. We have often heard the expression of the first Napoleon that the great need of the French people was mothers; and indeed the outbreak of the first French revolution presented a striking illustration of the neglect of the purifying influence of motherhood. When that outbreak occurred French society was permeated with vice; morals, virtue and religion were swamped in immorality. The corrupt plays of the theatre commanded the attention of the people. Maternity came to be looked upon with reproach; true family life, true home life was gone; and as a consequence Napoleon's words were more than justified, that France was really motherless.
Now, Mr. Speaker, let us apply the conditions which destroyed those nations in the past. What does the lesson teach us? Does it not teach us that if a nation is to be great and is to continue to be great its very heart, the home life of its people, must be good? It must be virtuous, clean, self-sacrificing and true. What are we going to do in this young country? We have been the leader in many avenues of national and international life. But what is the truth with regard to divorce? The year 1883 was the first in which divorces were recorded in two figures; the number that year was 13. In 1903 there were 21 divorces; in 1909, 51; in 1913, 60; in 1918, 114; in 1926, 608, and in 1927, 748. It seems that the bulk of the applications before the senate to-day are from the province of Ontario, my own province. But I am proud to say that so far as my own section of the country is concerned, so far as my own riding goes, I do not know of a single case of divorce. As regards my section of the country, I wish that condition to continue. I will not be a party to the passing of a resolution or a bill in this house to establish a divorce court in my province, let this house deal with the matter as it will.
From the arguments which I have put forth thus far you can clearly see that my purpose is to do away with the condition which saps the manhood and the womanhood of this country at its very foundation. As I said in my opening remarks, marriage is a sacred institution. Marriage is the key to the home and the home is the bulwark of the state and of society. If we continue to desecrate marriage through divorce we sap the real foundation of society, and I for one intend to vote as I have expressed myself, against establishing divorce courts in this province.

Mr. Speaker, this is one of the bills which might be affected by the amendment to the rules proposed this afternoon, and this is one of the many reasons why I am opposed _ to that amendment. The matter is a most important matter from almost every point of view, and so far as I am concerned I am prepared to vote against this bill for three principal reasons.
In the first place I am opposed to the principle of divorce. In the second place I believe a bill of this kind should be made general in its application if passed by this house at all. There are six provinces of Canada which at present have divorce courts, while the provinces of Quebec, Ontario and Prince Edward Island have none; if a measure of this kind is to be passed at all it should be generally applicable to these three provinces. The third objection I have to the bill is that neither the province of Ontario nor anyone on its behalf has ever asked for this legislation.
On Friday evening we had a rather long and somewhat diverting speech in this connection by the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa). In the beginning of his speech he pointed out clearly and positively that personally he was opposed to divorce and that the divorces granted by parliament had been passed against his will and over his protest. Further on, at page 384 of Hansard, I find that he used the following words:
.. .we shall be making a grave mistake if we vote for this bill as it stands, without making it clear that we are not imposing it upon the people of Ontario, in the absence of any opportunity on their part, and on the part of their own representatives in their own legislative governing body, of signifying their will. If we impose the bill upon them under such conditions we shall, first, encroach upon the moral rights of the people of Ontario, and, secondly, drive another nail into the coffin of our constitution, because we are again discharging one of those abnormal functions of intervention which have worked to the evil of the country and to the evil of the province affected every time this has been done.
I contend that parliament has no right to pass this act and that there is not the least occasion for it. The arguments put forward by the hon. member for West Hamilton (Mr. Bell), whose legal opinion I value highly, do not appeal to me. The first reason he gave for supporting the bill was because of the delay which sometimes occurs through which certain would-be divorcees are debarred during the current session from obtaining the redress to which they think they are entitled. I might point out that this often occurs in courts of law; I have known cases to go over from one term to another and then, when all

48S
Divorce Court-Mr. Hocken
the legal gentlemen were ready, the court would adjourn for the long vacation. These delays occur in our courts as well as in parliament. The hon. member also claimed that there was a discrimination between the rich and the poor. I understand that the cost of a divorce is not very great, and in most cases where the senate committee finds the party is unable to bear the expense it is cut down to the bare cost of printing, with no further charge. Will the hon. member or any other legal gentleman tell me that the cost will be less in a court of law? From the little experience I have had with cases in court I firmly believe that the present procedure is not more costly than would be the case if the procedure were changed.
One-third less.

I believe it is now one-third of what it would be then. The argument with regard to the procuring of evidence would also apply exactly the same in a court of law.
I am firmly convinced that the great majority of the members of this house are opposed to this bill; they are opposed to the general principle of divorce, and why should we as the parliament of Canada force the province of Ontario into this situation? If we are going to do it at all why not include all those provinces which at present have no divorce courts? Why single out Ontario for this legislation with no request from them? For my part I am prepared to vote against this bill on every occasion.

speakeroldname: Mr. H. C. HOCKEN (Toronto West Centre):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am one of those
who deplore as much as anyone in this house the situation with which we are faced, but I propose to vote for this bill. If my hon. friend from South Huron (Mr. McMillan) were consistent and logical he would move for the abolition of divorce courts all over the country, and that necessarily must be the position of any person opposed to the principle of divorce. As the last speaker pointed out we have divorce courts in six provinces of Canada, and if those who are opposed to the principle of divorce were logical they would move for the abolition of these courts and the prevention of divorce under any circumstances.

I would point out that
this parliament could not pass such an act; those courts were established under the British North America Act.

Then I would propose
that my hon. friend would be willing to accept the British North America Act for the province of Ontario as well as for the other prov-
inces, with all the privileges and rights given those other provinces.
I am supporting this bill not because it will make divorce cheaper or because I believe it will facilitate divorce, but because I believe that before a tribunal of this kind more substantial justice will be given the different parties. I have no criticism to make with respect to the committee of the senate, but consider their position: They are down here for a few months of each year and have to deal with hundreds of divorce cases. They must sit day in and day out and even break up their committee into two or three sections in order to deal with these cases, so under the circumstances divorces go through without the consideration they would get in a court of law. So I say I believe more substantial justice would be done in a court of law than is the case at present.
I am not opposed to the principle of divorce, although I am quite as firmly convinced of the sacrednes of the home and of marriage as my hon. friend from South Huron. There is nothing finer in this or any other country than a happy home, but where you find a home where a mother has deserted her husband and children and gone off with some other man to the United States is it fair to hold that husband to that position for the rest of his life? He may be a young man of only thirty or thirty-five years of age; should he be condemned to remain in that condition because of the weakness of his wife? On the other hand take a home where the man has gone off with some other woman, deserting his wife and family. If that woman can find some person with whom she thinks she can be happy why should she not be free to reestablish her home with a man who will be better to her and more honest with her than the one she first selected?
Will my hon. friend allow a question? What about the children of the first marriage; are they to be considered?

for me to forget as it is for some of my hon. friends opposite.

I do think that my hon.
friends from Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, if they associate themselves with this discussion, should not put the province of Nova Scotia or the port of Halifax in the position of refusing what is being done in all good faith in an endeavour to carry out the recommendations of that report. The Duncan report recommended the appointment of a harbour commission; it was appointed and last year we made a loan of $500,000 to that commission. This resolution proposes a further loan of $5,000,000, and my hon. friends are not putting the province of Nova Scotia in a fair light before the whole country when they continually harp on the question whether or not this is the exact form in which the Duncan report described the assistance which should be given these ports. The point is that the money is to be granted and these ports are to be carried on in a businesslike and efficient way. The commission was appointed in order that there would be some body which would have an opportunity and be in position to get business for the port, and to provide facilities to both the shipper and those who provide bottoms for the purpose of carrying freight. This body was to work out a coordinated program for the development of that port, and it has endeavoured to do so.
I do not think it adds anything worth while to the discussion to harp continually on the question of whether the Duncan report has been carried out in its exact form. As a matter of fact, if you read the report with relation to these ports-and I have taken pains to ascertain this from other sources as wrell as the report itself-you will find that it was intended that these ports should be dealt with in a similar manner to that in which the other great ports of the Dominion were treated. It has been suggested that these ports are going to be damaged. A government would be foolish to adopt methods whereby ports which had been conducted in the way my hon. friend describes would sud-78594-32
denly find themselves injured by the establishment of such a commission. It would be nonsensical and idiotic for a commission to carry on their work in a way which would drive shipping away from the port. I want to say to my hon. friend, and say to this committee, that I do not subscribe for one moment to the doleful wails which come from time to time from our friends opposite, who are bound to look a gift horse in the mouth, as it were, and see if there is not some way in which they can accuse this government of not dotting every I and crossing every T in connection with the Duncan report.
My hon. friend the acting leader of the opposition (Mr. Guthrie) raised what seemed to me to be a new question with regard to this matter; he selected the vote to the harbour of Halifax as the object of an attack on this government for extravagance.
No, I did not; I said the aggregate of these votes.

He selected this resolution which is now before the committee. I did not hear him make any complaint before, but when it comes to the harbour of Halifax that is the time when hands must be raised and shrieks uttered to indicate that this government has started a riot of extravagance. I want to say that if every resolution and every item in these estimates is as fully justified as the vote for the harbour of Halifax, then I think there will be no complaint on that score. The words of my hon. friend's leader are still ringing in the ears of the members of this committee when he pleaded the other day for the expenditure of further large sums of money on certain works which were being discussed at that time. You cannot blow hot and cold at the same time.
My hon. friend the acting leader of the opposition raised another issue, and one which I am sorry to hear him raise. He does not generally do this, but in some way or other he seemed to have got off on a wrong tack. He asked where there was anything in this vote for the western provinces and for the great province of Ontario. He cannot vote money in one resolution for every province in the Dominion; we have to take one at a time. As has been properly pointed out by my hon .friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Cardin), there are specific resolutions on the order paper for railways in the west. A considerable portion of the western grain will pass through these eastern ports. I ask the province of Ontario through what ports of the Dominion of Canada they ship their goods of this time of year except through



Halifax Harbour Commission
the ports of Halifax and St. John. My hon. friend shed tears over the province of Prince Edward Island, but there happens to be a vote in the estimates for something like $3,-
500,000	for a car ferry for that province. The provinces are not being neglected, and I do think it ill becomes my hon. friend to seize this vote as an opportunity to talk about extravagance and complain about the expenditures which are being made. My hon. friend's expression was that the house should hesitate in connection with this vote.
Mr. Chairman, I did not say that; I said the house should hesitate and be staggered by the aggregate of these votes.

I accept my hon. friend's statement, but Hansard will show just what he did say. Let us put it in the plural, and say that he said "these votes" while we were discussing this particular resolution, but I think he was effectively answered by his own fellow member from Halifax (Mr. Quinn), by the hon. member for St. John-Albert (Mr. MacLaren) and by the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson). These hon. gentlemen have intimated that they are strongly in favour of this vote. Of course they are in favour, because it is a vote for a national port in the Dominion of Canada, a port which is absolutely necessary in order that the business of the Dominion should be carried on.
I am very much pleased that my colleagues in the government have agreed to putting this amount in the estimates and to making this advance to the harbour of Halifax. If my hon. friend the acting leader of the opposition had been in Halifax during the last few months and had seen the development there, had realized that the Canadian National ships are sailing from that port to all parts of the world, had realized the West India service is proving such a success, had known that the great steamship lines are making Halifax their turning point, then he would have realized that this house is fully justified in the vote which is proposed to be made by this resolution. I am glad to support it, and I am glad, as I said a moment ago, to be a member of a government which recognizes the importance of this port and which does not do any cheese paring when dealing with a port which has the merits of the port of Halifax.

Mr. Chairman, in no way did I limit my remarks to the port of Halifax, and no one in this committee understood that I did. It happened to be on this particular vote that I spoke, but my remarks were directed entirely to the aggregate expenditure 
proposed by the government, and not in regard to these four or five harbours. I referred to the aggregate expenditure proposed in regard to railway extensions, and the point I intended to make and did make was that it was time to call a halt. I mentioned the fact that the expenditures for harbours on the one side, and railways on the other, called for guarantees of about $57,000,000, and in addition to this amount there had been estimates placed before the house amounting to $400,000,000. I realize that the expenditure in respect to the port of Halifax is an attempt to carry out the recommendations of the Duncan report, but it is time that someone called attention to the manner in which this government is piling up expenditures. That is what I intended to do and what I hope I succeeded in doing, and I repudiate the suggestion that my remarks were in any way directed against the port of Halifax.
I do not propose to be lectured by the hon. the Minister of National Defence. I think I have read the Duncan report as often and as carefully as has the minister.
I suggest that my hon. friend read it again.

I will do that when it suits me to do so and without any advice from the minister. I may read and later refer to it so often that he will regret having referred to it. I think I understand the language of that report, and I submit, as I have already stated, that the action proposed to be taken now is not in accordance with the recommendations of that report. So far as "harping" on this commission's report is concerned, or "whining," which is the language -of another of the hon. minister's colleagues -I want to say that I am perfectly willing that my attitude and his should be loft to the judgment of the people of Nova Scotia.

I regret very much that the Minister of National Defence has become so stirred up over the rather mild criticism which has been offered from this side of the house with regard to the development of the ports of Halifax and St. John. The house is to be congratulated on the fact that we have been getting along so nicely; that legislation has been moving so rapidly, and that the policies of the government are being worked out by both sides of the house in such an harmonious manner. We are all pleased with the development that has taken place at the ports of Halifax and St, John, and also with the fact that the White Star

Railway Act
line has given up the terminal of Portland, Maine, on the Grand Trunk system and has adopted Halifax instead. That suggestion, I think, came largely from this side of the house, and it was pointed out that the government had acquired the Grand Trunk-
I understand it was my hon. friends on that side of the house who voted to purchase the road to Portland.

I was coming to that. After the amalgamation of the roads in days gone by and our being put in possession of the Grand Trunk railway which runs down to Portland, we were in a position to talk to the White Star people and to see whether it was possible to divert to a Canadian Atlantic port the traffic which was going to Portland. I am glad toi note that has been done and the White Star line, after a successful test made with the steamer Regina, decided that Halifax would be in future their port. I am sure we on this side of the house are very much pleased with the efforts that have been made and the success that has been attained in this regard, in that the ports of Halifax and St. John are being recognized and that the government of the day, by improving them, is still further recognizing them. I hope in the near future the Minister of Railways will see his way clear to take the matter up with the management of the railways and see whether the grades cannot be lessened over that portion of the Canadian National Railways known as the Intercolonial where the grades are at the present time a little high. If that can be accomplished, we would have heavier trains passing through, and our Atlantic ports would be recognized more than they have been in the past.
I wish to point out to the Minister of Railways and the Minister of National Defence that the time is coming very rapidly when it will be almost unsafe on this side of the house to offer any criticism at all. We have been so far particularly mild on this side, but I can assure the government that there are points in connection with the recommendations of the Duncan commission that have not yet been carried out. As far, however, as these ports are concerned, we, as maritimers, are very much in accord with the stand which has been taken by the government in regard to their development.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Cardin thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 69, to provide a further loan to the Halifax harbour commissioners.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Railways and Canals) moved the second reading of Bill No. 60, to amend the Railway Act.
Explain.

This bill contains several amendments. The matters dealt with in it are unrelated to each other, and it is therefore rather difficult, on the second reading, to discuss any one principle. The procedure I thought of suggesting to the house was that the whole bill might be referred, after discussion on the second reading, to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, there to be examined without prejudice to discussion on the part of any hon. member at a later stage in committee of the whole. I will just run over the objects of the amendments proposed in the bill.
The first amendment deals with a matter discussed at the last session of parliament, namely, that of tolls on international bridges. It will be remembered that last session there was some discussion as to difficulties arising through various authorities having power to regulate tolls on international bridges, and I gave an undertaking on behalf of the government that we would look into the matter, and, if possible, propose a solution. The solution which is proposed in the first amendment in this bill is that all tolls on such bridges, however incorporated in the past, whatever the terms of the legislation presently existing may be, will ' in future be under the control of the Board of Railway Commissioners in the same manner as all other tolls.
The second amendment deals with a matter also discussed at the last session, and places under the control of the Board of Railway Commissioners the issue, sale or other disposition of increased capital stock of any company, the tolls of which are subject to the approval of the board. In that connection I would just say that the proposed amendment is of great importance and far-reaching in its effects. I am advised that a number of institutions coming under the legislation desire to make representations with regard to it, and I presume those representations will, if that is agreeable to the house, be made to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.
The third amendment deals with the subject matter of the resolution passed a day or two ago, extending the provisions relating to contributions to the grade crossing fund for a further period of ten years at the rate of $200,000 a year. I gave some information when the resolution was before the house and if the bill goes to the railway committee it will be possible there to summon the officer?
Railway Act

of the railway commission and to go into any phase of the administration of the grade crossing fund.
The fourth and fifth amendments are made at the request of the Board of Railway Commissioners, and are technical in character, designed to facilitate the filing of tariffs and reduce the number of tariffs to be filed in certain cases. I am advised by the board that, in order to comply with the law as it at present exists, it is necessary for companies to file as many as 170 documents in connection with one particular item of freight traffic. The recommendations of the board have to do with simplifying the procedure in that regard.
The sixth amendment deals with a question much discussed last session, having to do with companies which are subsidiary to companies at present within the range of the act. My hon. friend from South Toronto (Mr. Geary) has a bill now before the railway committee dealing with this matter. During the recess the law officers of the department and of the railway commission and of the Department of Justice have been giving attention to the best manner in which to effectuate the purpose which was the subject of so much discussion last session, and which is now made a part of this bill. The method of obtaining the objective is unlike the one adopted by my hon. friend from South Toronto. The proposal in this bill is more far-reaching. It embraces all the companies falling within the purview of the act, but I think it will be found to be completely satisfactory so far as effectuating that purpose is concerned, if parliament desires to have that purpose effectuated. I submitted the proposal to the railway commission with the question as to whether they would have under these amendments with respect to subsidiary companies all the powers necessary to enable them to make any investigation into their affairs which the carrying out of the act would necessitate, and the answer was that the amendments proposed, and as contained in this bill, would enable them to do what was desired in that regard.
I think that covers all the proposals contained in the bill. While I am, of course, prepared to listen to a discussion of any of them, I am debarred on the second reading from speaking again and from answering questions, and I suggest that it would be more convenient to discuss the amendments at another stage. I just wish to advise the house that it is my intention to move that the bill be referred to the railway committee, in order that an examination of all the details of the bill can be there made.

I have listened with a good deal of

interest to the explanation of the minister, and I have read the bill with some care. The bill is involved and to some extent technical, and I think the suggestion of the minister that it be now read a second time and be referred to the railway committee for further consideration is a very wise one.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and referred to the select standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.
