maintopic: WAR REPARATIONS PAYMENT OF $2,500,000 TO CUSTODIAN
speechtext: Before the resolution goes to the committee, there are some remarks that I wish to make. We are in the somewhat unusual position of having a resolution introduced by the minister, setting aside $2,500,000 for certain purposes connected with reparation claims, and we are completely in the dark as to what is meant by the resolution. As I understood the minister's attitude when the resolution was first moved, he refused to give information.

maintopic: WAR REPARATIONS PAYMENT OF $2,500,000 TO CUSTODIAN
speechtext: No, that is not fair

maintopic: WAR REPARATIONS PAYMENT OF $2,500,000 TO CUSTODIAN
speechtext:
I asked him when he was on his feet to give the house some explanation as to his proposals. The only assumption we can make is that -in setting aside $2,500,000 the government is setting aside a sum that is insufficient to pay the claims in full. Whether the minister may say later that the 12,500,000 is being set aside as a payment by way of instalment, I do not know, but I am going to assume for the moment that this amount is being set aside not as an instalment, but as the final dealing of the government with the question of reparations; that the government is setting aside $2,500,00, as was intimated by the minister, as an act of grace towards those who suffered loss by reason of enemy actions during the late war.
I had occasion last year to refer at some length to this matter. It is not my intention to go into it fully now, but there are a few remarks relative to the subject which I feel ought to be repeated in order that the house may have a clear understanding of the situation.
We have in the consolidated revenue fund of this country to-day, or had last year, the sum of $10,800,000, which has been received as payment on reparations from Germany under the treaty of Versailles. We should have to-day in the consolidated revenue fund, if Germany has made her payments during the year, approximately $15,000,000, because the payments of reparations by Germany to Canada are fixed at approximately $5,000,000 for an indefinite period of years. Those payments are made, if at all, by reason of one fact only, namely a contract made between this country, as one of the allied nations, and Germany, and that contract is known as the treaty of Versailles. Those payments are being made under article 232 of the treaty of
Versailles, and at the risk of repetition I want the house to listen again to that article.
I shall read only a portion of it:
The allied and associated governments, however, require, and Germany undertakes, that she will make compensation for all damage done to the civilian population of the allied and associated powers and to their property during the period of the belligerency of each as an allied or associated power against Germany by such aggression by land by sea and from the air, and in general all damage as defined in Annex I hereto.
The first thing to which I wish to draw the attention of the house is that obviously the whole spirit of that section is the payment of civilian damage, whether it be damage to property or to life or to health. Added to it is " in general all damage as defined in Annex I" of the article. Now Annex I contains some ten subsections, eight of them relating entirely to the individual and only two of them relating to the state. One of those two is of no consequence, and the second relates to the payment of pensions on the French scale.
We have received money from Germany under that contract, and in no other way; and the whole spirit of the contract is that this money is paid as compensation for civilian losses during the war inflicted by Germany or her allies. We have received to-day, as I pointed out in the beginning of my remarks, approximately $15,000,000. lhat is one side of the picture. We have received that money from Germany under a contract, and it is ear-marked for a certain purpose.
The other side of the picture is this: Have we ascertained the claims for which that money has been paid by Germany? I need not take you any further back than the report of Mr. Friel, which was filed with the government on December 27, 1927. I may say in passing that last year the excuse which the Secretary of State offered for not dealing with the matter was that the government had not had time, that they only received the report late in the session. But they had the report of Mr. Friel in their possession on December 27, 1927, the date which it bears, or one month before the session began.
By this report Mr. Friel found that some sixteen hundred people in this country are entitled to payment of claims in full under article 232 of the treaty of Peace. Those sixteen hundred people have coming to them a total amount in round figures of $4,246,000. He has recommended the payment of interest at five per cent in the case of property loss from the date of the loss, in the case of all other claims from the date of the ratification

IVar Reparations-Mr. Ernst
of the treaty of Versailles by this parliament, January 10, 1920. With interest those claims amount to-day to approximately $6,500,000. According to the figures which the Secretary of State tabled last session they amounted then to just a little over six and one-quarter millions of dollars.
Now, sir, we have the complete picture. We have fifteen million dollars in the consolidated revenue fund of this country received from Germany, and we have the claims ascertained at six and a half million dollars, with interest. Why, then, is the government setting aside two and a half million dollars to pay these claims? Why not the six and a half million dollars which are requisite to pay them in full?
The attitude which the minister took last session was this. He said: we are going to follow the practice of Great Britain. Because they made ex gratia payments, we are going to make ex gratia payments, or charitable donations, if you choose to call them such, to those who suffered loss by enemy action. He also said that the provisions of article 232 of the peace treaty had been abrogated at the conference of the Spa in 1921, so that that article, in popular parlance, went by the board. I ask hon. members if they ever heard of a contract between two individuals abrogated by a bargain made between two other individuals. Suppose I make a contract with the hon. Secretary of State, can I abrogate that contract by entering into an agreement with the member for Inverness? Yet that is what he is saying in relation to article 232 of the treaty of Versailles. He cannot produce anything to show the house that Germany is paying one cent to this country or to any other of !the allies, with the exception of the United States, under any other arrangement than that set out in article 232 of the treaty of Versailles; and in the case of the United States Germany pays under a separate treaty which contains exactly the same provisions.
Great Britain's course was what? Great Britain in 1920 set aside five million pounds, which was applied towards payment of necessitous claims in the first place, and on a sliding scale towards payment of all other claims. But for two reasons the case of Great Britain is not parallel with ours. Firstly, when Great Britain set aside five million pounds she was setting aside her own money; she had not received any from Germany. In the second place, Great Britain requisitioned all her shipping during the war. It was under the control of the state; the state insured it, and
I Mr. Ernst.]
if a ship was lost the insurance company paid the policy money. In other words, if the owner lost his ship he did not lose the value of it; he received compensation. But in this country the shipping was carried on by private individuals, and if a ship went down the owner had to bear the loss. Consequently, as a majority of our claims are claims for shipping losses, there is no parallel between the situation in Great Britain and the precedent which the minister finds in the action of the British government, and our own situation.
Let us take the record of the government itself. The action of Great Britain dates back to 1920. In 1925 this government surely was aware of the precedent which had been set up by Great Britain, yet in 1925 they appointed Mr. Friel to investigate these claims. They were also aware of that precedent in 1923, when they appointed the late Doctor Pugsley to investigate claims falling within article 232 of the treaty. I ask the house to bear with me for one minute while I turn to the commission of Doctor Pugsley. This is the first paragraph:
Whereas, in and by an order of our governor general in council, bearing date the thirteenth day of March, in the year of Our Lord, 1923, (copy of which is hereto annexed), provision has been made for an investigation by our commissioner therein and hereinafter named and report upon all of the claims set forth and referred to in the said order in council hereto annexed, for the purpose of determining whether they are within the categories in the first annex to section one of part eight (reparation) of the treaty of peace with Germany, and the fair amount of such claims, and to make such findings as may be of assistance to the government of Canada in determining w'hieh, if any, of such claims should be paid and the extent of payment thereof, and for the purpose of considering and recommending to the custodian of enemy property releases where the parties are necessitous, suffering and in hardship.
I draw the attention of the house to these words:
-to make such findings as may be of assistance to the government of Canada in determining which, if any, of such claims should be paid, and the extent of payment thereof,
In the first place, Doctor Pugsley was appointed to investigate claims falling within article 232 of the treaty of peace. In the second place, he was appointed to determine the fair amount of the claims in order to assist the government in deciding what they should do. Doctor Pugsley's appointment,
I may say in passing, was three years after the action of Great Britain, which is now set up as a precedent. In 1925, when Mr. Friel, was appointed, the recital in the commission

War Reparations-Mr. Ernst
reads in part the same as that given to Doctor Pugsley, but the last words are different:
"Whereas in and by our certain letters patent under the great seal of Canada, bearing dates respectively the thirteenth day of March and the twenty-first day of May in the year of Our Lord, 1923, a copy of which is hereto annexed, we did nominate, constitute and appoint the late the Honourable William Pugsley, in his lifetime of the city of St. John in the province of New Brunswick, to be our commissioner to investigate and report upon all the claims^ set forth and referred to in the orders in council of the thirteenth day of March and the twenty-first day of May, 1923, copy of which was annexed to our letters patent respectively, and all claims which might be submitted to our said commissioner for the purpose of determining whether they are within the first annex to section one of part eight of the treaty of Versailles and the fair amount of such claims.
Now I ask the house to note the change in the wording. In this case Mr. Friel was appointed to investigate claims falling within article 232 of the treaty of peace, and he is appointed to recommend the fair amount of such claims. The words:
.-as may be of assistance to the government of Canada in determining which, if any, of such claims should be paid, and the .extent of payment thereof-
-have been deleted from the recital, and obviously they have been deleted for a purpose. That purpose was that the government at that date thought it would be bound to pay what Mr. Friel recommended. That is obvious from the fact that on the very day of issue of Mr. Friel's commission Mr. Copp, then Secretary of State, introduced into this house a resolution providing for payment of Mr. Friel's awards. How in face of that declaration of policy can the government come here and say to-day:	"We are going to
provide two and a half million dollars in payment of claims which with interest aggregate six and a half million dollars"? It is changing the whole policy of the government, and changing it, I submit, without reason.
Mr. Friel in the course of his report recommended that all these claims be paid in full with interest on property loss from the date of loss, and on all other claims from the date of ratification of the peace treaty by this country. Now, sir, in addition, to that, when Mr. Friel was appointed, as also when Doctor Pugsley was appointed, there were other significant words in the orders in council. In both orders the German government was given the right to have counsel appear before both Mr. Friel and Doctor Pugsley on the investigation of these claims. I ask the Secretary of State, what interest has the German goveminent in a charitable donation by this government to the citizens of this country? Why was the German government allowed to have counsel, indeed, asked to have counsel before the reparations commissioner if it was not because the government felt bound by article 232 of the treaty of peace?
It is not my intention to labour this question at great length, but I submit that we have in the United States an exact parallel to our own case. The treaty of peace between Germany and the United States contains a provision which is identical with our article 232. The United States last year provided for the payment of its reparations claims in full, and to do so they required $191,000,000. They did not have enough German reparations money and so they took $50,000,000 of their own. They took a large sum from the enemy property fund and paid in full all claims up to $100,000, and provided, in respect to the larger claims, that payment would be made in full as the money was received from Germany. Their situation being precisely the same as ours, they present an exact parallel; and if the government are looking for a precedent in this instance I would ask them to look, as they so often do, to the south of the line and not across the water.
But apart altogether from the equity of the matter, I submit that there are moral reasons why these claims should be paid. I know that the minister will probably reproach me with confusing issues if I refer to the enemy property fund and the payments made out of that fund. But we had in this country, and we have to-day, a very considerable fund made up of sequestrated German property and debts due from the people of this country [DOT]to German nationals, and the distribution of that fund falls within articles 296 and 297 of the treaty. Broadly speaking, claims under the treaty can be made against that fund only in the case of detention or destruction of property within the boundaries of Germany during the war. Let me give an example. At the outbreak of the war the Thompson Shipping Company had two vessels tied up in Hamburg, where they remained during the war. That company were able to claim under article 296 of the treaty, and they received an award of $1,300,000 from the mixed tribunal which sits in London, so that the government of this country paid out of the enemy property fund that sum in settlement of the Thompson Shipping Company's claim. What is the difference morally or in equity between the case of the Thompson Shipping Company and that of Besco-or the Scotia company,

War Reparations-Mr. Cantley
a subsidiary of Besco-which had five vessels sunk on the high seas during the war? Are we to give the Thompson Shipping Company 100 cents on the dollar and, relying upon a technicality, give to the Scotia only 10 cents? Is that equitable or just?
Take another case within article 296. The Massey-Harris Company had a large amount of property sequestrated in Germany, in respect to which they received $300,000; while The T. Eaton Company had a large amount sequestrated in Amsterdam, outside the bounds of Germany, and so it did not fall within either article 296 or 297. The T. Eaton Company had to rely on article 232. The Massey-Harris Company received 100 cents on the dollar; an<l are we going to give the T. Eaton Company 10 cents? I ask the members of this house whether that is reasonable or just. Can we make fish of one and flesh of the other? Having considered ourselves bound by the provisions of articles 296 and 297, are we going to say that in this case article 232 is not applicable? Let me tell the house further that in the case of disputed claims, where there is no claim under 296 or 297, and where the claim has only been asserted, the German government pays 15 per cent in settlement. Now are we going to be worse than the German government, which pays our nationals 15 per cent on an unfounded claim, and pay to our own people, on claims which are just, only 10 cents? But there are other moral reasons besides.
Take the situation in my own constituency * and I know that the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff) will corroborate every word I say. A large number of fishing vessels were sunk there during the war; the submarines got amongst the fleet and destroyed the vessels.	These vessels are
operated on the share basis: the men go to sea in the ships, relying for their pay on the proportion of the value of the catch to which they are entitled. Many of these ships were sunk, in many instances when they contained their catch, so that the men lost their season's earnings. The vessels are more or less community owned; many of the men who sail in them are shareholders.	The commissioner
recommended the payment of property loss as well as payment on account of lost earnings; he also recommended compensation as solatium in the case of men who were set adrift sometimes hundreds of miles from land in open dories. In many instances these men came home penniless. Some had to mortgage their homes to get along or had to be carried by the local merchants. They had to pay interest on the money they borrowed to tide
TMr. Ernst.]
them over the period to which their earnings would have applied. They paid interest on that money, and are they not to be compensated for the loss they have sustained? I appeal to the government therefore, even at this late date, to amend this resolution so as to make payment not only of 100 cents on the dollar but also of interest, as recommended by the commission. In so doing, the government would be only doing justice, and tardy justice at that.

speechtext:
I
wish to support the claim made by the hon. member who has spoken (Mr. Ernst). I am surprised at the action taken by the government in this matter. In New Glasgow one of our ships, of about 5,500 tons, was taken over by the British government and was later sunk in the Mediterranean. The owners were paid the full value of that vessel years ago as was done in cases referred to by the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Ernst). Take the case of half a dozen ships or more owned by the Scotia company of New Glasgow: we owned or -controlled some 75,000 tons or more of shipping at the beginning of the war and at its conclusion had but one vessel left. We had a steamer carrying railway cars to Vladivostok, built at New Glasgow for the then allied Russian government; owing to the collapse of the Panama canal she had to be sent through the Mediterranean and the Suez canal. That ship was torpedoed south of the island of Crete, the crew being turned adrift. They were adrift some five days in wintry weather, finally landing on the south of Crete, after one of the boats was upset in the swell and its occupants thrown into the water. Now that is only one case out of several. Had these vessels been taken over by the British government, as was another New Glasgow-owned steam vessel, full compensation would have been made and that years ago. There was only one reason why they were not so taken over by that government; they were employed almost solely in the transport of railway cars or other material for use of the British government or the allies. Their charter value at that time, according to the rates paid other steamers, would have been quite $200,000 per month. As yet we have not received a penny, and now the Secretary of State proposes to pay us 15 per cent of our loss. Is there anything fair, is there anything just, is there anything reasonable in that proposition? I leave it to the house.

maintopic: WAR REPARATIONS PAYMENT OF $2,500,000 TO CUSTODIAN
speechtext:
I rise at this stage to protest against the principle involved in this resolution. The

War Reparations-Mr. Ladner
very able addresses of the last two speakers leave little to be said, if it is possible to convince the government of the wisdom, even at this moment, of changing their course. There is another aspect of the question. I had intended covering some of the points made by the last two speakers, but will not need to do so. However, I would like to point out the injustice, the unfairness and the lack of consideration on the part of the government with respect to Canadian citizens as compared with the treatment received by citizens of the United States, Great Britain and Germany. There is the case of a company -which insured vessels carrying produce across the ocean; the vessels were sunk, the goods lost and the insurance paid. The insurance company is subrogated to the ranks of the claimants. In the United States, under the act known as the Settlement of War Claims Act of 1928, the rights and merits of these claims were fully investigated and an act was put through providing that claimants of this kind, wffio actually sustained the loss, should be reimbursed to the extent of one hundred cents on the dollar plus interest.
Part of the work in Canada had been done before Commissioner Friel was appointed. I know of one case where Commissioner Pugsley brought down a judgment which was not officially reported, favouring the claimant. Mr. Friel inquired into the whole Question again and came to the conclusion that the claim should not be allowed because of a technicality which is . not recognized in any other country; in other words, equitably and legally he was entirely wrong. I understood that it was the intention of the government some time ago to provide for the right of appeal to the exchequer court; large sums of money and consequent far-reaching effects upon business make it right and just that something more than the authority of a commissioner of the government Should be final in matters of this kind. Why the government have changed their course I do not know; they seek to appropriate $2,500,000 now, with the inference that this is the final distribution, notwithstanding ithe fact that the government have in hand approximately $15,000,000 of German money under the Dawes plan whidh, by all rules of common sense and ordinary understanding, was intended to reimburse the nationals of this country. I think the forceful argument of the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. ' Ernst) not only demonstrates that point but is overwhelmingly convincing in the conclusion he drew.
Now I put it to the government: On what ground of reason, fairness or justice to our own people whom we normally seek to protect can the government refuse to use this money for this purpose? In addition to that they have some $12,000,000 iij the hands of the custodian of alien property, which under certain conditions would be available to our nationals. It seems to me that instead of aiming to protect and reimburse our own people for whom they are trustees, the government are seeking to deprive Canadians of the money and rights to Which they are justly entitled through the depredations and the inhuman conduct of the enemy during the war; they are depriving our people of these things and extending to Canadians a treatment which the citizens of no other country are obliged to receive. I do not put it stronger than that, because I do not think it is the intention of the Secretary of State to throw deliberately upon the people of this country who were injured as a result of the wrongful acts- of the enemy an injustice which cannot be defended in a court of law, in parliament or before the bar of public opinion.
There is just one other aspect of the case. I appeal to the government to carry out the understanding, whether official or unofficial, that the right of appeal to the exchequer court would be established. These claims, involving large sums of money, should not be left to the judgment of one official of the government; there should be a right of appeal to some court and I submit that the exchequer court is the proper place. I want to draw the attention of the government to the case of the Lusitania, which covers some of the points with which I am concerned, and which was considered in the United States before the umpire of the Mixed Claims Commission, whose judgment was as follows:
The Lusitania -was freighted with persons and with personal property. Germany's act in destroying her caused the loss of the ship, some of the lives, and practically all of the property that formed her cargo. The lives that were lost and the property that was destroyed entailed economic losses to the world, to the nations to which they belonged, and to the individuals owning or having an interest in the property or dependent for contributions upon the physical or mental efforts of those whose producing power was destroyed by death. The aggregate amount of the property lost became fixed when the ship sank and is neither increased or diminished nor in any wise influenced by the amount of the insurance or reinsurance thereon. The insurance becomes material only in determining -who really suffered the loss. This is because a contract of marine or war risk insurance is a contract of indemnity ingrafted on and inhering in the property insured.

War Reparations-Mr. Ladner
The extent of the liability thereunder is limited by the economic loss suffered. The insured suffers no loss to the extent of payments made him by the insurer, who is the real loser to the extent of such payments not reimbursed by reinsurance.
That is an,extract from the decisions given by the Mixed Claims Commisison in the United States. I have had brought to my attention, among others, one claim of some substance which comes exactly within the principle of that decision, a principle which has been followed in Great Britain, and I submit that in the face of the finding of the commissioner, wherein he bases his decision against the law and against the equities as they are determined in other countries, nothing could be fairer than that the applicant should have the right of appeal to some other tribunal for final decision, where perhaps he would be given greater consideration both as to the law and 'as to the merits of the case.
Without involving the rule to which you referred, Mr. Speaker, may I ask the minister now if it is the intention of the government, before the completion of this matter, to afford an opportunity for appeals of this kind to be presented, or is the present motion the final action on this question?
